utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We're continuing with the Prosecution. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning. Allow me, please, to -- before we start, just to introduce that today Defence for Dr. Simic is appearing with our young and bright colleague, Mr. Jason Moore from Houston, from South College of Law. Thanks to the arrangements from registry and the colleague from Houston, he's here in the capacity of intern and he did great contribution to our work in the drafting and preparing of our briefs. So I'm very pleased to have Mr. Moore with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. You're welcome, Mr. Moore, to the Trial Chamber. We'll proceed. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. In the remaining time, there are several miscellaneous matters from yesterday which I would address the Trial Chamber on before I turn to sentencing. Unfortunately, I didn't prepare a -- and I -- an outline this morning, but I can tell you what the four -- or the five areas are. One is the analysis of the evidence of Mr. Paleksic in relation to Dr. Simic's evidence. The second one is references in Mr. Zaric's book to which the Prosecution says the Trial Chamber should pay particular attention. The third area is the report of retired General Wilmot, that's a very quick one. The fourth one is an observation on a legal matter, the underlying acts. The fifth is several observations on the exchange and exchange system and document P128, which is the instructions from the Prime Minister, and the last one is sentence, and I'll cover those matters within the remaining time. The first matter to which I direct Your Honours' attention is the evidence of Mr. Paleksic, who the accused Dr. Simic called in his defence in January this year. The Prosecution's submission -- this is an important witness whose evidence the Trial Chamber should scrutinise with great care. Part of Dr. Simic's defence, as the Trial Chamber is aware, is that he objected when he found out about what -- it is unclear exactly what he found out from his testimony. He objected to some of the activities of Mr. Todorovic, who, of course, gave quite lengthy testimony in these proceedings about his own activities and his own breaches or serious violations of international humanitarian law when he was serving as the Crisis Staff's police chief. The evidence of Dr. Simic - and this is at pages 12420, 12421, and also at 12581 to 2 - is that he spoke to the police chief, Andrija Bilosevic, and with members of the Ministry of the Interior in relation to Todorovic's activities. The summaries which Dr. Simic provided in relation to Slavko Paleksic seem to suggest that he was the person who was going to give evidence about the visits or the inspection of the Bosanski Samac police station at Dr. Simic's initiative. In his evidence, Dr. Simic, at 12582, referred to an inspection and the establishment a "commission," because the Ministry of the Interior has inspectors, its own inspectors, and he established a commission of inspectors that came to Samac to check the work of Stevan Todorovic in the Ministry of the Interior. That commission stayed and it sort of peters out there. The suggestion if that a commission was established to oversee the work of Todorovic and Paleksic was going to be the person who enlightened the Trial Chamber as to Dr. Simic's humanitarian and political concerns about Todorovic's activities. Now, of course, Paleksic, though Mr. Paleksic, as the Trial Chamber heard, is a former judge, public prosecutor, a municipal secretary, and after the war, he was even a Minister of the Interior of Republika Srpska. He was also a man who actually worked as a legal assistant for Dr. Simic on this case, and one whom one might have expected to provide some favourable evidence, at least evidence in -- correlating to the summary provided. However, Paleksic's evidence is important as to what actually did happen, and it's important in relation to the Prosecution's submission about the nature of the enterprise in Bosnia, as implemented in Bosanski Samac through the various participants of the police, the Serbian police, the MUP, the Crisis Staff, the military, and so on. Paleksic testified as to five investigators arriving at the Bosanski Samac police station. Paleksic was responsible for "legal affairs," he said. Two of the other investigators dealt with police matters, one with criminal investigation issues, and another was dealing with financial matters. The evidence was remarkably vague, one would think, in relation to this crack team of investigators arriving, descending from the Ministry of the Interior upon this regional police station to investigate matters of some concern. Now, the date of this is very important in terms of Prosecution's submission. Paleksic's evidence was that it was in December 1992, and the visit was a three- or four-day visit. This is important because it must have been after Dr. Simic received his copy of the 13 signatories exhibit, that is, P127, which is dated the 1st of December, 1992, and the evidence, which seems to be uncontested, is that the meeting between the Crisis Staff, or members of the Crisis Staff, and the signatories on the 2nd Posavina Brigade occurred within days. So at the most generous estimate for Dr. Simic, there may have been an overlap between his being informed and that meeting and the arrival in Bosanski Samac of the team of inspectors. Now, of course, as you know, in P127, one of the allegations which is detailed -- which is outlined is of "the massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims without any criteria," and some of the prisoners, of course, these are the prisoners in Todorovic's custody, being subject to measures such as abuse, torture, or even killing, characteristic only of war criminals of Ustasha origin." Todorovic, as the Trial Chamber is aware, testified to and admitted to and was pleaded -- and pleaded guilty to and was sentenced for crimes occurring in the police station, the very same police station that was supposed to have been investigated in December 1992, crimes occurring before, murder, sexual assault, repeated beatings of prisoners, unlawful arrest, detention, confinement of Bosnian non-Serbs, their cruel and inhumane treatment, other crimes, of course, occurred outside of the police station, but they were crimes which the Prosecution submits were well known in Bosanski Samac to almost -- or to everyone. What was Paleksic's task? Well, his task, as he said it, was to investigate irregularities in the issuing of drivers' licences. And in his three or four days in this inspection of the torture chamber, otherwise known as the Bosanski Samac police station, he found over 100 transgressions as far as the issuing of drivers' licences were concerned. That was at page 1 -- sorry 13281. The result of his inspection was that he found that people were being issued drivers' licences without proof of their taking a driving test. And as far as Paleksic was concerned, the former judge, public prosecutor, Ministry of the Interior official with a war assignment, in charge of personal and legal affairs at the Doboj regional supervising station, as far as he was concerned, this team of which he was a part was not investigating any of the matters in the indictment to which Todorovic had pleaded guilty, not even the more minor ones in the scale of things to which he had pleaded guilty, that is, the beatings, as opposed to the torture or the murders or the sexual assaults. Mr. Paleksic heard nothing about Todorovic's well-known and notorious activities in that police station during his visit. And most significantly, and most significantly for the defence of Dr. Simic or the defence he a attempted to mount is that Dr. Simic never mentioned a thing to Mr. Paleksic, his star witness, as to the investigation in the police station, at his instigation, he says, about any of the matters referred to in Mr. Todorovic's testimony, about any of the matters for which he was sentenced, even, as I said, earlier, the most minor ones. Now, the Prosecution's submission is that the only conclusion the Trial Chamber can draw from this is that even Dr. Simic's own witnesses don't support him on this point and he was not telling the truth when he gave his evidence before this Trial Chamber. And what was the result of the inspection, apart from the finding of the 100 or so driving licences transgressions? Well, the supervisor, Blazanovic, was appointed for about three months to supervise such things as how they were going to treat citizens. Well, one would hope not to murder them. And the dress code, that's at page 13828. Again, another important aspect for the Prosecution's case is that Todorovic, a murderer, assaulter, torturer, and member of the Crisis Staff, remained in this position for some years afterwards. He remained in his position as the chief of the Bosanski Samac police station after having committed the gravest breaches of international humanitarian law, not to mention domestic laws, for the balance of the indictment period, the end of 1993 and several years afterwards. There is not a shred of evidence before this Tribunal that Dr. Simic, who simultaneously maintained his position at the same time as Todorovic as president of the Samac municipality, that he did anything or used his offices or used his influence to bring Todorovic to justice for anything, any of the many crimes, the daily crimes, that Todorovic committed while in the police station. The only justice Todorovic is faced with is before this Tribunal. The only inference the Prosecution says, from that is that Simic approved of the crimes that Todorovic committed as part of the joint criminal enterprise. Another matter which I'll swiftly deal with is the report of General Wilmot, retired General Wilmot, which is D182/1, tendered by Dr. Simic. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber should disregard the report almost in its entirety, with the exception of pages 16 to 28, which, as the Prosecution has outlined to the Trial Chamber before, were basically plagiarised from a report of an OTP a military analyst, Mr. Butler, as to the subordination within the Bosnian Serb army. Those parts may be peripherally relevant to subordination issues, if the Trial Chamber needs to look at subordination issues, but otherwise the report is irrelevant. It's made by a person with no qualifications permitting him to offer any historical or political opinions on historical or political matters, unlike the two well-qualified Prosecution experts, Drs. Gow and Donia. And in this respect the Prosecution asks - and we apologise for our omission in our written final trial brief - to incorporate the submissions we made in our motion of the 24th of April, 2003, in relation to the weight and the relevance of retired General Wilmot's report. The Prosecution notes in relation to a matter I brought up yesterday on how the Trial Chamber should deal with the underlying acts charged in support of -- or charged to support the charges of complicity in the indictment at paragraphs 11 and 12. The Prosecution asked the Trial Chamber to deal with proof in this manner. We asked that -- or we submit that the Trial Chamber only has to find participation in one of the underlying acts established to prove participation in persecution. The Trial Chamber does not need to enter a finding of guilt or acquittal in relation to the underlying acts, and most significantly so because some of them may not be crimes in their own rights. The Prosecution says the appropriate finding would be a finding, if the Trial Chamber is satisfied we have proved our case in relation to any of them, a finding that the Trial Chamber is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the accused's involvement in whichever underlying act, and therefore is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt and can convict of the count of persecutions as a crime against humanity, or -- I'm sorry - persecutions as a crime against humanity. The Prosecution says it is not necessary and the Trial Chamber should not acquit on those underlying acts but the Trial Chamber is certainly entitled to find that they're not satisfied that the Prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt in relation to any of those particular matters. The Prosecution also -- I also wish to add so several matters from our analysis of the exchanges yesterday and make these following points, and we urge the Prosecution to view the exchanges or the exchange system as part of the overall campaign or system of persecutions in place in Bosnia-Herzegovina as implemented in Bosanski Samac in the indictment period. And we ask the Trial Chamber to scrutinise especially the evidence of Milutin Grujicic, who was the person most qualified - that's Mr. Tadic's witness - to speak about the interplay and the coordination between the various Exchange Commissions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Republika Srpska, in the indictment period. The Prosecution emphasises that Grujicic's evidence establishes the organised and systematic nature of the exchanges and that it was highly coordinated, it was coordinated amongst the six different corps of the VRS, including the 1st Krajina Corps and the East Bosnia Corps, which was in the Bosanski Samac area, and Mr. Tadic's Exchange Commission was an integral part of the overall exchange system which was operating in Bosnia at the time. And in this respect, the Trial Chamber -- the Prosecution reminds the Trial Chamber of the Special Rapporteur's report, which we've referred to, as paragraph 138 of our chronology, and the conclusion. That's the Special Rapporteur's report of the 27th of October, 1992, that the Special Rapporteur finds "widespread and serious human rights violations continued to be committed in Bosnia and intensified in certain respects, killings, beatings, rapes, destruction of houses and sacred sites, threat, pressures, and terrors. The Muslim population are the principal victims and virtually threatened with extermination." And we emphasise this: Ethnic cleansing is not the consequence of the war but is its goal. To a large extent, it had already been achieved. And we ask the Trial Chamber to use the words, the report of the Special Rapporteur on the ground in Bosnia in the indictment period to support the Prosecution's case and its allegations of the exchanges as part of the ethnic cleansing, as part of the persecutions. While I'm on the chronology, there are two things which the Prosecution wishes to amend, and we will file a revised chronology. There were two paragraphs which should not be in the chronology. They slipped in or they didn't slip out during the proofreading. They're paragraphs 81 and 108. And we ask that the Trial Chamber to disregard those, that's 81 and 108, for the moment. We will file a revised one as soon as possible. And paragraphs 63 and 64 are on the wrong side of the page and one of them is out of order. We will also attend to those particular matters. The Trial Chamber -- I withdraw. The Prosecution didn't address yesterday on P128 and due to an omission it was also slipped out of the final trial brief in proofreading, and that is an important document to which we ask the -- to which we refer your attention and ask you to scrutinise very carefully as part of the Prosecution's case of an organised campaign and the links between the Bosnian Serb leadership and the Bosanski Samac municipal leadership and the manner in which the persecutions were carried out, and that is P128, which is the instructions for the work of the municipal crisis staffs of the Serbian people, issued by the Prime Minister, the Republika Srpska Prime Minister, on the 26th of April, 1992, and referred to at paragraph 90 in our chronology. We ask the Trial Chamber to take into account all of the instructions there and how they fit into the Prosecution's case of the systematic and widespread nature of the persecutions. The Prosecution also refers you -- I won't take you to the passages, but I refer you to the following pages in Mr. Zaric's book, which is P180 and P180A, and we ask you to scrutinise these particular pages or give particular pages to them, at pages 127, in which Mr. Zaric refers to the strategic significance of the Posavina corridor; page 142, when he refers to before the takeover, why shouldn't the Croats try to make up for Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Vlasenica right here; pages 148 and 149 regarding the establishment of the Crisis Staff and the Serbian municipality and the announcement and how we say those passages support the Prosecution's case; page 152, where he refers to weapons collection on the 17th of April and that members of the Serb police will be used in places where resistance is possible or probable, which the Prosecution says supports its case; page 154, where he refers to the method of collection by the paramilitary units, where he says weapons for them were the secondary interest and a mere cover for robbery; and at page 154, where he refers to talking to Mr. Radovan Antic, then commander of the 4th Detachment, telling him to call Nikolic, those guys are looting all over the town, and Antic's response: "I've heard what he said. Tadic has reported the same thing," which the Prosecution says corroborates the Prosecution case that Mr. Tadic was in fact involved in weapons collection on the 17th of April, contrary to his own evidence. And of course the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. You mentioned page 154 twice. Was that your intention? On line 3, page 11, line 3, and then anew on page 11, line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour. There were two passages on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. And this I take it is from the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Page 157, referring to the prearranged nature of the arrests, starting with, "the arrest, detention, and confinements are a special chapter in the longest day in the recent history of Samac and that people must be arrested from pre-prepared list," that passage; page 160, where Mr. Zaric refers to an attack from the village of Prud: "Early in the morning there was a minor attack more in the nature of an incident really," which the Prosecution says supports its case that there was no attack from Prud or no threat from the Muslims or Croats; page 169, where Mr. Zaric refers to spending the next few days at the MUP, preparing for his interrogations of the important politically or persecutorily detained prisoners. This particular passage is important in relation to the evidence -- Mr. Zaric's own evidence of finding P71, which is the isolation order, at the Bosanski Samac police station after -- had to have been after the 15th of May, which was the date of the order being made, and seeing the document in three different offices; page 200, exchanges and isolations at Zasavica, where he says: "I was soon to learn the use value of human beings and the price of their heads and the calculation of ethnic leaders." The Prosecution says that goes to his knowledge of the system of exchanges as persecutions at the time, which is contemporaneous with his involvement in negotiations in relation to prisoners from Odzak; also at page 201, where he refers to -- it was his -- refers to the telephone call to Alija Izetbegovic, and Mr. Zaric says that it was indeed his suggestion, Mr. Zaric's suggestion, to call Mr. Izetbegovic, and then he says: "So we brought Alija's relative, Izo Izetbegovic, to make the call," which the Prosecution says corroborates its own case and Izetbegovic's evidence as to what happened; and page 203 in relation to the Odzak exchanges; and page 217, in relation to - I may have quoted this - the role of the paramilitaries, where he said: "We did not begrudge them the recognition they deserved." I think I quoted that to him in his evidence. The Prosecution asks you to scrutinise that passage; and finally at 243, where he refers to an interview with Croatian journalist and ethnic cleansing, and the fact that it had occurred on both sides. We ask you to especially scrutinise those pages. I finally turn to one matter before the sentencing which will only take me a moment, and that is the evidence of Professor Nikolic, who was the -- of course, you heard Dr. Simic or the joint defence constitutional expert. We ask the Trial Chamber to particularly look at pages 12165 -- well, 12164 to 7 in relation to the activities which were pleaded in the indictment and which the Trial Chamber has heard much evidence and which the Prosecution said has established beyond a reasonable doubt, and the fact that Professor Nikolic says each of those would be unconstitutional under the Republika Srpska constitution. And that can be used in relation to a finding that the matters complained of were illegal as a breach of a law or a law or a human rights document. Finally, I turn to the subject of sentencing. The Prosecution makes the following submissions in relation to all three accused. They are set out quite comprehensively in our final trial brief. During the indictment period, the Crisis Staff, as the Trial Chamber has seen from the document I just referred to, P128, basically controlled all aspects of life in -- life and work in Bosanski Samac. The Crisis Staff, and then the War Presidency, issued hundreds, if not thousands, of orders affecting every aspect of life of the inhabitants of Bosanski Samac during the indictment period. As we have outlined and as you have heard, they implemented an unimaginable system of persecutions against the non-Serb population, culminating, the Prosecution says is established by the evidence, in their forcible expulsion from their homes and the municipality. The Prosecution has established beyond a reasonable doubt that each of the three accused participated knowingly and willingly in these most serious and grave breaches of international humanitarian law. For their willing participation in what we have described as ethnic cleansing, the international community demands severe and salutary punishment, as retribution and deterrence for what occurred, for the crimes of the accused. Several matters we draw your attention to at the moment: In sentencing, upon a finding of guilt, the Trial Chamber should consider, from the evidence you've heard, the long-term effects on the numerous victims of the persecutions and deportations in Bosanski Samac municipality. The Trial Chamber has only heard but a representative sample of what the victims experienced and endured and what many are still experiencing and enduring to this very day, including the -- the Trial Chamber heard of their long-term psychological, physical, and even economic effects, where people still don't have their homes and lost all their possessions, the long-term devastating effects on the victims of the accused's egregious crimes. They are aggravating features in common to all three accused. These aggravating features, the Prosecution says, are firstly, the willingness of their participation, which the Prosecution has established from the wealth of evidence of the control exercised by the Crisis Staff and the participants in this enterprise over the lives of the unfortunate victims of their campaign. Secondly, the -- sorry - the duration of the conduct. With Mr. Tadic and Dr. Simic, it was right to the end of the indictment period. The Prosecution, of course, says that with Mr. Zaric he was no longer part of it. The Prosecution concedes, after December 1992. The duration of his participation is not as long but is nevertheless significant in the scheme of persecutions. The Trial Chamber should also consider as an aggravating feature the educational background of each of the three accused and their role as community leaders before their participation in the persecutions and deportations. All three were educated, and Dr. Simic, of course, is a doctor of medicine, and the Prosecution says, and the case-law supports, that this aggravates their conduct. These were people who knew better and should have known better. Turning to Dr. Simic, Dr. Simic is a doctor engaged in conduct which was repugnant to his humanitarian training. He, as you have heard, was at the apex of the system of persecutions and deportation in Bosanski Samac. He was one of the architects. He was one of the main people employed in implementing the persecution on the ground through the most insidious methods in Bosanski Samac. There are no mitigating features in relation to Dr. Simic. He has shown a complete lack of remorse for everything that he did and indeed everything that happened. Not only does Dr. Simic deny any wrongdoing at all, he appears to deny any knowledge, apart from attempting to blame everything conveniently on Todorovic, who of course has pleaded guilty and has been sentenced and can be safely blamed. The Trial Chamber is also entitled to consider the fact that he has not cooperated with the Tribunal in its valuable work, attempting to promote reconciliation in the former Yugoslavia and to bring justice to the victims and to bring to justice those responsible for these most serious violations of international humanitarian law. The Prosecution submits or recommends that Dr. Simic deserves a severe and salutary sentence of over 20 years imprisonment. The range we recommend is between 20 and 25 years. Turning to Mr. Tadic, Mr. Tadic, of course, like Dr. Simic, was also a respected person in his community, a school teacher, a cafe owner, a prominent local personality. He used that position and he used that position for his ideological and personal gain during the war, during the indictment period. He took on a key role in persecuting and deporting the non-Serbs. Without Tadic or Tadic's, people willing to take on the role of deporting, expelling people from their homes, the ethnic cleansing could not have occurred in Bosanski Samac. And Mr. Tadic most cynically, the Prosecution says, attempted to portray himself as a humanitarian, helping those unfortunate people in their prison cells, to escape from the horrors of life. The Prosecution says nonsense. He was an integral part of the system. Like Dr. Simic, there is no real mitigation in relation to Mr. Tadic's behaviour. He too has shown no remorse. He too has failed -- has not cooperated in this Tribunal's most valuable work. But an additional aggravating factor in relation to Mr. Tadic is the abundance of evidence that he personally benefitted from the misfortune, the agony of those imprisoned, those who were desperate to pay their way out of the torture and persecution that they were suffering. The evidence of his soliciting and accepting bribes, large sums of money, jewellery, gold, in times when the economy was shot, so to speak, and those were the most valuable trading commodities. The evidence was he was one of the wealthiest people in Samac before the war. Well, the evidence is he was after the war too. And the Trial Chamber should find the reason is because of his acceptance of bribes from those desperate to leave the hell hole that Bosanski Samac had become for non-Serbs. We ask the Trial Chamber to find as an aggravating feature Mr. Tadic's personal benefiting from the misery of those victims. For his role in the persecutions and deportations, the Prosecution also recommends a severe and salutary sentence designed to deter those who may engage in these practices in the future. We recommend a sentence of at least 15 years, between 15 and 20 years. Finally, turning to Mr. Simo Zaric. Mr. Simo Zaric was also a community leader. He, of course, was a former chief of public security. He informs us that he was the youngest ever appointed in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a man whose job had been to uphold the law for many years, a man looked up to in his community, a man about whom his fellow Serb citizens spoke highly. He too willingly participated in the system of persecutions and exchanges. He had his place in that system. It was not as great. It was a lesser role than the architect of the system in Bosanski Samac, Simic, and the chief deporter, Tadic, but it was a role that was nonetheless significant in the scheme of things in a small municipality. The system of persecutions required willing participants like Zaric at every level; otherwise, it could not have been successful and as successful as it was in ensuring that there were almost no Muslims or Croats left in the municipality by the end of 1993, when there they had previously been a majority of the population. There are no mitigating circumstances in relation to Mr. Zaric either, in relation to his participation. He too has not cooperated with the Tribunal in its valuable work in the former Yugoslavia. He has, of course, expressed apologies to the victims, as the Prosecution supposes he really had to when faced with the evidence, his interviews, and his own book. His apology was for what happened to the victims, but there is not one word of remorse spoken for his own role in this, nor even an acknowledgment of his own not insignificant role in the scheme. The Prosecution submits that even if the Trial Chamber were to find his guilt established as an aider or abettor, which of course you could, as opposed to a principal participant on the evidence, or even as an aider and abettor, his role was significant in furthering the system the enterprise in Bosanski Samac and the deportations of the non-Serbs. In his role too, he should receive a salutary and severe sentence. The Prosecutor recommends a sentence of at least 10 and up to 15 years. The Prosecutor also submits in relation to all three, if you cumulatively convict, as we have said you can and submitted you can, you must bear in mind the principle of totality in sentencing for all three offences, and our submissions of 20 to 25 for Dr. Simic, 15 to 20 for Mr. Tadic and 10 to 15 for Mr. Zaric are made in that light. Those are the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We now turn to the first defendant, Dr. Blagoje Simic's Defence, for their closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone. First, Your Honour, allow me to deal with some housekeeping matters. In fact, after the reviewing our brief, due to the typing errors, we found that the reference to certain exhibits in the number of footnotes does not correspond. So just for the record and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and our learned friends from the Prosecution, I'm speaking about the footnote 17. Instead of P109/1 and elsewhere in the brief, it should be "D." Obviously, when we have /1, we know that this exhibit relates to Dr. Simic. But there was just an error between the letter "P" and "D." So instead of "P," it should be "D." Then same applies to footnote 18, 28, 50, 52, and then also typing error in footnote 677, instead of letter "Y," it should be "T," as in transcript. Same applies to footnote 682 and 683. Also, whenever in the brief when the Defence makes reference to the exhibits, it should be also added "ter," because when we are speaking of exhibits, we are speaking in totality of English version and B/C/S version. And then small error in our table of contents. Instead of "section 7," it should read "part 7." And also, Your Honours, during the work on our pre-trial brief - sorry - closing brief, we found certain inconsistency between the electronic version of transcripts and so-called hard copy version of transcripts. Namely, after the page 18814, if someone is reading electronic version, the page number should be deducted for six pages, after the page 18814. Otherwise, all references made in our brief are actually based and related to the hard copy transcript that we usually receive from the registry after the every day of proceedings. I believe that this discrepancy covers, let's say, seven or ten days in May, mostly through the testimony of Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, for these corrections, the Trial Chamber would suggest that you file a correction page for all the corrections, so that it is attached to your briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but in fact I made a correct version. My version is based on the documents that I'm receiving from the registry. But I notice that my learned friend from the Prosecution, they make reference to the electronic version. So I'm working from the documents that I usually receive from the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your attention, Your Honours. Blagoje Simic. Blagoje Simic, Blagoje Simic, Blagoje Simic. We heard on numerous occasions in the submission of the Prosecution name of my client. And then like the echo in my ears, I hear only first three letters of his name, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. And then today when is the birthday of Dr. Simic we heard the present -- certain present from the Prosecution to him, but, Your Honour, allow me to deal with the case. Dr. Simic is not guilty. He is not guilty because he was not involved in any activities that would constitute a crime, be it under the domestic or international law. Yes, he was a member of Crisis Staff. Yes, he was a member of SDS. And yes, he was the speaker of the Crisis Staff. But in his capacity, he was never involved in any of the activities that the Prosecution had alleged and tried but failed to prove throughout this trial. Who was Dr. Simic back in that period? He was by all means an archetype, a young man from humble beginnings from the area, who worked very hard and very diligent in becoming and finishing medical school. Returning back to the area where he was born to help his fellow citizens and members of his community. You heard testimony how he specialised in the field of medicine. One of his primary contributions was providing service to all of the citizens and residents of this community with chemodialysis, be they Serb, be they Muslim, be they Croat. He did not discriminate. To appreciate the situation, you have to look at Dr. Simic not through what was happening throughout the war, but also what was happening before the war, before the April of 1992. We have to look at country that shook itself from the grips of Communism and was in transitional process into a democratic society. This is indeed significant because with this new situation, members of the educated class found themselves with the particular obligations in becoming a part of this movement, of these changes. So it was not unusual that someone with Dr. Simic's educational background, being an esteemed member of the community, would get involved in politics. And so at age of 30, he joined SDS, and soon after he was elected to the position of the vice-speaker of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac. Who would have thought that Dr. Simic could never have imagined that within a short period of time a war would break out, that would in many ways polarise the community structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or is it because he was already in politics because of his level of diligence in commitment to his public service, that when the situation become necessary to form a Crisis Staff, he was asked to do his civil duty? It needs to be underscored that the concept of forming of Crisis Staff was not unique in this area. It was not unique to B and H and it was not unique throughout the various parts of the former Yugoslavia. The concept of forming of Crisis Staff had been around for decades, and it was a means of dealing with various crisis, natural disasters, or emergencies on an ad hoc basis at the local level. It was a well-known term within the world history, most recently after the tragic days of 11 September in New York. And in fact, we have heard that all sides - the Muslims, the Croats, as well as the Serbs, throughout B and H - formed crisis staffs, because this war created a crisis in every single community, and Bosanski Samac was no different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm waiting for the B/C/S translation. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your, I think, opening couple of lines, and I also note in the written brief that you are referring to Dr. Simic as being the speaker of the Crisis Staff, the speaker of the War Presidency, and so on, and also vice-speaker of the Municipal Assembly, and so on. I can't seem to find the paragraphs here, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Now, in parliamentary systems that I'm familiar with, the speaker has a very special function, and I'm just a little bit confused, because in the joint statement of admissions by the parties and matters which are not in dispute, concerning Dr. Simic - this is on page 12, paragraph 90 - we have the word "president" being used, vice-chairman of the Municipal Assembly, president of the Crisis Staff, president of the War Presidency, and so on. The only reference to speaker I can find is in the last sentence, concerning being elected speaker of the Samac Municipal Assembly and serving in that position until 1996. So I wonder whether you could explain to us what is the significance of your repeated use of the word "speaker" in the brief, in contradistinction to what's in the joint statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do that gladly. Since we are coming from the different legal systems, I must give certain interpretation, although we made that in our closing brief. And actually, contrary to the Western standards -- I'm speaking about Canada or United States - where we have a position and function of mayor of the town, and he is superior to the police and all other services in town. At that time, in system of Bosnia-Herzegovina and elsewhere in former Yugoslavia, there was no such function. It was introduced only recently, through the High Representative for Bosnia a couple of years ago. So now in Bosnia we have a speaker of municipal parliament, which is exactly the same function as we know who speaker is in the Western parliamentary systems, and now we have a mayor in Bosnia, appointed by the higher authorities, et cetera. It is rather similar, Your Honour, I mean, term "mayor" with burgmeister that you can find in Rwanda, namely in most recent case of Bagilishema, who was acquitted for certain crimes, although I will come later to that. So in Europe, in western Europe, we have the term "mayor" which name is burgmeister in Germany, and that is exactly the function which is similar to mayor. On the contrary -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But I wasn't referring to mayor. I'm referring specifically to use of the word "president" in the agreement by both parties, the Defence and the OTP, dated 27th April 2001. There's no mention of mayor in paragraph 90. It's referring to Dr. Simic as president of the Crisis Staff and president of the renamed War Presidency. So that's what I would like you very briefly to address, the difference in the terms "president" versus "speaker."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In addition to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- That question, even the exhibits which are before the Trial Chamber, accepted by Dr. Blagoje Simic as having been signed by him, title him as president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we are reading -- if we are reading the provisions of the statute, municipal statute, we could find exactly what is the scope of activities of we can use this word just hypothetically president of Municipal Assembly. The theological [sic] approach is that actually the term "president" in Municipal Assembly throughout the system of former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia, means speaker. So in order to, to some extent, to better explain function of Dr. Simic, I'm using term "speaker" because speaker is actually what, according to the municipal statute and the other provisions in the law, is the case. Let me remind you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help you, instead of using so many words. Please answer this question. When you are talking speaker, president, or whatever, did Mr. Simic in his different capacities have a vote, in case the votes fall even, he had the decisive vote? Please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: He didn't have a vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He has a vote but he wasn't able to get so-called casting vote or decisive vote or golden-share vote, whatever you want. So he was first among equals. He was assemblyman, he was elected assemblyman among the 50 of assemblymen of Municipal Assembly and they voted him to be speaker of that Municipal Assembly with the same power, I mean vote for Dr. Simic and all others was the same. So.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: You know, in addition, when playing with these words, in the Western systems, the speaker has no vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. But I said that it's rather a mixture between Western and Eastern systems. What counts is the role and scope of chairman or speaker of the Municipal Assembly as stated in the statute of the municipality. So we have to go to read his functions in statute of municipality and then we shall see -- also we can -- we have to make some references to Professor Nikolic's statement and then we shall understand what was the role of Dr. Simic within the constitutional system of former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina. So for the -- my understanding from the function that he performed and from the words -- from the statute of the municipality, that actually he was speaker, not mayor. Because let me remind you, Your Honours, that in previous stage, Dr. Simic was charged with 7(3) Article responsibility, but they dismissed the charge on basis of 7(3), specifically due to the provisions of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska with regard to his function. Because the perception in 1995, when initial indictment was filed, was from the Western point of view that he was a mayor, which was not the case. Thank you. So when the municipal department of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska assigned him this position in accordance with the applicable law - I'm speaking about his function, being speaker of the Crisis Staff and member of the Crisis Staff - consequently, he found himself in the position of the speaker of the Crisis Staff. In fact, on 18 and 19 April 1992, there was a - we received the evidence - there was a gathering of duly elected municipal assemblymen, in order to find appropriate solutions to face the extraordinary circumstances that were confronting them. The Prosecution would have us believe that the Crisis Staff was a joint criminal enterprise. It would have us believe that it was formed for the purpose of ethnic cleansing. It would have us believe that someone, somehow, it was an exclusive authority, above all other authorities, where other institutions and organs, such as police, and even the military, were subordinated to this Crisis Staff. They would have us believe that everything that occurred in Bosanski Samac during the period covered by the indictment was directed or planned or organised, supervised, carried out, by the Crisis Staff and Dr. Simic himself. The evidence simply does not bear this out. Even their own witnesses cannot substantiate these claims. But before I go any further, let us be clear about several matters. The indictment does not claim that being a member of the SDS is a crime. The indictment does not claim that organising a Crisis Staff is a crime or that being a member of the Crisis Staff is a crime, or the existence of a Crisis Staff is a crime. As I said earlier, the indictment does not charge Dr. Simic under Article 7(3). And so if the police department, as the Prosecution claims, was under the authority of the Crisis Staff and was directly under the authority and control of Dr. Simic, then surely the Prosecution would not have deleted the charge under Article 7(3), as originally they had charged him in the first indictment, as I mentioned earlier. Furthermore, the indictment does not charge Dr. Simic of being a member of joint criminal enterprise. The fact remains that he's not charged with joint criminal enterprise in a manner and method and language used by the Prosecution in other cases here in this Tribunal where explicitly joint criminal enterprise is the heart and soul of the charge. The Defence addressed that issue in its brief to some extent, and the Defence doesn't want to give any particular expanded response to that, because simply, the joint criminal enterprise was never charged in this case. That's an intention, intentionally or unintentionally, I'm not -- that's job of my learned friend, the Prosecution. But that's the case, Your Honours. So when we look at all the evidence that the Prosecution has put forward, when we look at the lack of evidence which we would have expected from the Prosecution to put forward, their failure to challenge certain evidence, such as, for example, the handwriting expert, with respect to the document concerning the isolation. I'm speaking about the Exhibit P71. And even the Prosecution agrees that it cannot be proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Dr. Simic signed this particular document. When we look at all what has been brought before this Trial Chamber, we can only reach one inevitable conclusion: Dr. Simic was not involved in persecution. Dr. Simic was not involved in ethnic cleansing. Dr. Simic was not involved in isolation or deportation, or starvation or inhumane treatment, or any other charge listed in the indictment. He was not in charge of or in control of or had authority over the police and the military or the criminal warlords, such as the Prosecution star witness Stevan Todorovic. Dr. Simic was not involved in rounding up various members of the community for the purpose of exchange. He was not involved establishing and running detention centres. He was not involved in any form of discrimination when he came to exercising his duties and his functions, limited as they were, as the speaker of the Crisis Staff. And while it is undisputed that certain members of that community did in fact engage in certain criminal activities, Dr. Simic was not one of them, directly or indirectly, and the evidence bears this out. Madam President and Your Honours, I have divided my oral presentation in three parts, the first part being the contextual aspect to this case, which I have already touched upon, which is the Bosnia-Herzegovina Posavina region and municipality of Bosanski Samac. Then I will go to my next section when I will discuss briefly the law and evidence. And finally, the last section will be on the Prosecution's main witness, Stevan Todorovic. And then I will conclude with some summary remarks, tying our entire case and summarising both my oral and written submissions. In the light of the time constraints and given the Trial Chamber's generous allotment for the presentation of the written submission in which we believe we have dealt with all aspects of this case in a very concrete manner, I will not go into all the facts, because they have been covered with specificity in the written submission. But before I begin my first part of my oral submission, Your Honours, I prepared for your convenience an analysis of the Prosecution brief, and addresses the Prosecution arguments. It's rather an outline sort of road map for -- that you can use which I trust will be helpful and you can collate and synthesise my written and oral submission along with the record in this case. So I kindly ask the assistance of Mr. Usher, please. I have copies for the Trial Chamber. I have one copy for the Prosecution and for the Court, obviously. So Your Honours, you can see that actually the form is made on the basis of the Prosecution brief, the titles too, and then in each of these positions you can find at which paragraphs of Defence brief we covered that particular issue, although our brief in totality should be viewed in totality with regard to the case of the Prosecution. Thank you. I'm now starting with the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Posavina region and municipality of Bosanski Samac. And to some extent, with some reservation that I embark on this segment of my argument, and that is trying to understand the essence of this case, in the context of the political realities as they existed and as they evolved prior to the outbreak of the war. When Dr. Simic responded to the indictment by voluntarily coming here, as he believed was required of him to do so under the law, he did so with the understanding that he would be facing an indictment based on the facts and based on the principles of international criminal law, be they customary or statutory. However, as we have seen throughout this trial, the Prosecution has politicised these proceedings. They have done so by trying to demonise and illegitimise the creation of Republika Srpska, its citizens, who in the midst of the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia were attempting to realise their right to self-determination, just as the others in former Yugoslavia, such as Slovenes, Croats, Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Croats, and Macedonians. What the Prosecution has done in its case, and we see this in a rather chilly manner through its brief, just as they have done throughout the trial is to characterise Republika Srpska and its institutions including Municipal Assemblies as a shadow government, parallel government, and specifically in this case, as stated in their brief, private institution of Dr. Simic. Let me give you just a few examples of the language used in their brief. They repeatedly describe official institutions of Republika Srpska as rebellion by its nature. They used terminology such as Blagoje Simic's Crisis Staff, Blagoje Simic's SDS-controlled Crisis Staff, SDS-dominated Crisis Staff, Crisis Staff's detention centres, Crisis Staff's police, Crisis Staff's chief of police, War Presidency's secretariat for National Defence, et cetera, et cetera. That's the language that they are using. It is obvious that the Prosecution is desperate and in a state of panic, since they are not able to provide any sustainable evidence to prove their case. Using sarcastic and, to some extent, derogatory terms, they tried to create a foggy curtain behind which they hope to be persuasive. Your Honours, at this stage, allow me to respectfully bring to your attention some more significant issues that I believe are of the importance for the defence case. With certain reserve, I would say that I wish to invite all of you back to the days when the situation in Bosnia was very fluid, very uncertain, and dangerously explosive. In particular, I'm speaking of the fall of 1991, when in the night between 14th and 15th October, Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim MPs, violating constitutional and democratic principles, outvoted Bosnian Serb MPs by adopting several documents dealing with the crucial issues in terms of vital interest of the constituent nation and the statehood. The Defence thoroughly dealt with this topic throughout the trial proceedings and also in its brief. For the sake of expediency, I will not go into any greater details, but I would, however, like to point out that many learned scholars upheld the Defence positions. For example, one of the top UN officials, the eyewitness of the events in Bosnia, learned professor Susan Woodward, wrote a book, "Balkan Tragedy: Chaos and Dissolution after the Cold War." It is also worth mentioning that Professors Steven Burg and Paul Shoup wrote a remarkable book, "The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina: Ethnic Conflict and International Intervention," which is highly recommended even for foreign policy specialists and others interested in these events of Bosnia including State Department of the United States. And least but not last, there is a book, "Blueprints for a House Divided: The Constitutional Logic of the Yugoslav Conflict," dealing with the constitutional crisis in Bosnia and the author of which is Professor Robert Hayden. So in sum, the Defence position is that Bosnia-Herzegovina entered into the process of dissolution on 15th of October, 1991. This process lasted until the Dayton Peace Accords, reached in 1995. Throughout this process of dissolution, a parallel process of formation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was ongoing. Throughout the entire period between October 1991 and December 1995, three constituent nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed their institutions, administrations, and entities. It is therefore unacceptable claim of the Prosecution that Bosnian Serbs acted unlawfully and contrary to the constitutional and legal framework. The Prosecution tried to create a story that there was a central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They tried to create a fiction that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a state during the period covered by the indictment. They tried to convince this Honourable Trial Chamber and the public that Bosnian Serbs were rebellions. Your Honours, at that particular time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a state. Muslim-led presidency - I'm quoting word "presidency" - and other institutions were illegitimate and did not act on behalf of all three constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnian Croats established their own entities and institutions, and only in 1994, under the firm action of US state department, they reached so-called Washington agreement, with Bosnian Muslims, and then they formed Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an entity which at present time is part of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So from October 1991 until Dayton, Bosnian Serbs were in process of formation of Republika Srpska, and both Muslim Croat Federation and Republika Srpska, certain -- deferred certain competencies to the common institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina at these days, actually, after the Dayton, in accordance with Dayton. We have to know that both entities have their own armies, own police, own constitutions, presidents of republic and federation, parliaments, et cetera. So what conclusions may we draw from the Dayton Peace Accords? Because we have to look at the totality of this process. Number one, Dayton Accords recognised the legitimacy of Republika Srpska. That's the first point. Number two: Dayton Accords recognised the principle of protection of vital interest of constituent nation, and principle of safeguards of national interest in multi-ethnic states. Number three: The Dayton Accords clearly annul findings, political findings of the so-called Badinter commission. I'm speaking in particular with the opinion number 2 in para 2, where this commission found that Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia will have a right of minority, not constituent nation but minority, and that's why Dayton Peace Accord in accordance with the principle of international public law and in accordance with the principle pacta sum servanta is obligatory. It's a source of international law and it's clearly -- the findings in Badinter commission opinion 2, para 2, is clearly annulled by this source of international law. The Dayton Accords recognise the principle of two-third majority or supermajority if you like, enshrined in all civilised legal systems throughout the world and that principle was violated during the referendum of Bosnia-Herzegovina in February 1992. That principle was clearly violated during the adoption of the memorandum of sovereignty and other illegitimate acts by Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat MPs from October 1991 and onwards. And from the position of the Defence, we think that another turning point during the period covered by the indictment was the Lisbon agreement which was reached in February 1992. Leaders of all three constituent nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina called for a state composed of national regions for all three peoples, all three constituent nations. It was the Bosnian Muslim side - this is indisputable fact - that chose to repudiate the agreement. That was another step to descent into the war. And third and final step towards the conflict was politically motivated process of recognition of a state not being a state by the USA and European Union in April 1992. And then all Bosnia-Herzegovina descended into war. But let's go back to the municipal level of Bosanska Samac. Dr. Simic tried to act in favour of reconciliation and peaceful solution. When the Croatian community of Bosnian Posavina was formed in December 1991, and we have evidence in our case with that regard, it was more than obvious that the Bosnian Serbs in Bosanski Samac alarm bell was activated, since the municipality of Bosanski Samac was included in the political and military objectives of Croats and Muslims in the region of Bosnian Posavina. And in the eve of the outbreak of hostilities throughout Posavina region many Serbs were killed, many Serb women were raped, many Serb political leaders were assassinated. Many Serb religious institutions were destroyed. We heard the evidence to that extent in our proceedings. It was before the 17th of April, 1992, in Posavina region. As to the Bosanski Samac municipality, things were not better at all. SDA and HDZ formed their illegal, secret armed formations. They formed their military commands. They formed their secret crisis staffs. Finally, they planned to forcibly take over the municipal institutions by launching military attack in the period between 16 and 18 of April, 1992. And we have clear evidence to that extent. And only due to the fact that military intelligence of 17th Tactical Group obtained reliable informations pertaining to imminent attack of Croat and Muslim forces on municipality of Bosanski Samac, it was possible to react by launching a defensive military operation in order to prevent tragic consequences which already occurred elsewhere in Bosnia Posavina region. Although we could predict with greater precision what would have happened with Dr. Simic himself, his family, and other Bosnian Serbs living in Samac municipality in the light of the Posavina -- Bosnian Posavina events mentioned above, it is clear from the evidence that Dr. Simic played no role in military operations in the night between 16 and 17 of April, 1992. Your Honours, it is my deepest belief that we have to concentrate our attention to the criminal law issues, and the issues of criminal procedure. Although it's completely understandable that certain contextual aspects of the case, including public international law issues, constitutional law issues, and political issues should be discussed, it is nevertheless improper what the Prosecution pleaded throughout these proceedings. They tried to create a story based on wrongful premises. Firstly, they disregarded the causes for the dissolution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, they misunderstood the principle of self-determination of nations. And thirdly, they desperately tried to politicise these criminal proceedings by labelling the SDS party as a joint criminal enterprise. Fourthly, it is clear that they do not understand constitutional law system in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, and the role and competencies of municipal authorities within the legal system. And finally, they franticly tried to demonise Dr. Simic, accusing him of being a Serb SDS leader and ultimately a war criminal, simply because he was caught in the process of formation of Republika Srpska. And he was caught in a legitimate defence of his family and fellow citizens and the process of self-determination of his nation. Your Honours, if these actions are crime, then Dr. Simic is guilty, as millions of Serbs acted in the same way. Your Honours, it should be absolutely clear that nobody can be exonerated of his individual criminal responsibility if, in order to achieve the above-mentioned goals, this process encompasses violation of international humanitarian law. This is absolutely indisputable fact. But let me say clearly and loudly: Dr. Simic did not violate provisions of international humanitarian law. Your Honours, I believe it's time for a break, because now I'm going to the contextual basis with the Samac events, so maybe it's a proper time, because we're almost now time for a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. We continue. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before Mr. Pantelic resumes, I reluctantly make or ask the Trial Chamber -- or make this point. I try not to object during opponent's submissions out of courtesy. These are legal proceedings. It's not a political forum. During Mr. Pantelic's submissions before the break, on two occasions he accused the Prosecution of politicising the proceedings, just before the break he accused us of desperately trying to politicise the proceedings, in the course of his submissions. The Counsel for the accused is entitled to make submissions on the evidence and make submissions which are available from the evidence heard at trial or make legal submissions based on the law or international legal materials. He is not entitled, in the Prosecution's submissions, to make those sorts of allegations in this legal forum in the closing stages of the trial. Had there been a proper allegation of the Prosecution politicising proceedings, it could have been brought by a motion at an appropriate stage during the proceedings. The Prosecution asks Mr. Pantelic to desist from those sorts of comments and to concentrate on the legal issues and the submissions. He's entitled to criticise the Prosecution brief, the evidence, and make appropriate submissions in relation to those matters, but to go no further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. The Trial Chamber appreciates your intervention, but I wish to say that I think it's the way we understand these terms. It's different in different legal systems, and I'm sure that Mr. Pantelic does not mean to be mean with these terms approximate by describing the manner in which the Prosecution has tabled their case as meaning that it -- they tended to make it into a political debate or a political -- perhaps the Crisis Staff being a political institution or anything like that. I'm sure it's a question of the way we deal with the different terms, and I believe that Mr. Pantelic will, as his brief shows, has commented or has made his submissions according to the way he understands the evidence, and I don't think it's necessary for Mr. Pantelic to respond or explain anything, but please to continue with your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. That was exactly the position of Defence. Maybe it's term of presentation, it's maybe a word which was used. In any case, what we heard here during all the case here, that the Prosecution tried to label Dr. Simic as a member of SDS and therefore a member of the broader joint criminal enterprise simply because he was a member, and simply because certain -- members of SDS on the top-ranking position were indicted by the same office. So just in that term, I would like to distance this category from the proceedings. And I'm very -- I would like to -- I'm very grateful to you, Madam President. That's exactly what is the basis expressed in our brief, and throughout the oral submission. Thank you very much again. And before I continue, Your Honour, just allow me to make a short correction in page 24, line 22, instead of theological should be teleological. A form of interpretation. And then, I'm very grateful to my learned friend Mr. Moore. He just during the break informed me that in terms of the question posed by His Honour Judge Lindholm, just for the record, to say that speaker of the House of Representatives in US has a vote, so speaker has a vote, but not casting vote. Just for the record. And Your Honours, that I have laid out the contextual basis at the state level, let us go to Bosanski Samac and see what was happening there, because this is a case about Bosanski Samac. This is a case about Dr. Simic. This is a case not about, as I mentioned, the demonisation or delegitimisation of the Republika Srpska or SDS or members of these institutions. Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac was formed on 29 February 1992, pursuant to the decision of National Assembly of Republika Srpska, and in accordance with the Republika Srpska constitution and all other relevant legislation. That was the basis, legal basis. Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac was formed by the will of duly elected assemblymen from Bosanski Samac. Municipal Assembly operated in accordance with its statute, the rules of procedure, and within Republika Srpska legislative system. In its legitimate response to the imminent military attack by Croat and Muslim forces on the municipality of Bosanski Samac, the civil authorities formed the Crisis Staff. The role, function, and competencies of the Crisis Staff were defined by relevant legislation and the Defence has explained that in great detail in its brief. Bosanski Samac municipality, on 17 of April, 1992, and throughout the period covered by the indictment, was at the front line of severe battle between warring sides. Dr. Simic, being a duly elected civil servant, acted in his capacity as the speaker of the Crisis Staff. He did not possess casting vote or prevailing vote, or golden-share vote. He was first among equals. He acted in accordance with the principle primus inter parus. On many occasions he was outvoted by the other members of the Crisis Staff. His function was rather ceremonial or coordinative in terms of process of voting or adopting municipal regulations. What Dr. Simic did throughout the period covered by the indictment, more precisely, in the period between 17th of April, 1992 and the end of 1993? There is a clear evidence in this case that immediately after the outbreak of hostilities in the municipality of Bosanski Samac on 17 of April, 1992, Dr. Simic participated with other municipal assemblymen and officials in order to prevent humanitarian catastrophe of civilian population in Bosanski Samac. Due to the heavy shelling, lack of water supply, electricity, and general chaos caused by the armed conflict and violence, Dr. Simic did his utmost to provide food, milk, and to establish the state of public utilities at the acceptable level under the circumstances. He acted spontaneously. He acted in accordance with the Hippocratic oath and in accordance with his duty as a municipal civil servant, and he acted in a non-discriminatory fashion, where little resources were made available to all, irrespective of their ethnic background or their religious beliefs. The municipal Crisis Staff started officially operating on 19 of April, 1992. First adopted decision was the notification on extraordinary circumstances and introduction of a state of emergency. Nothing in this particular decision was discriminatory by its nature, and that is how the Bosanski Samac municipal authorities started their struggle for well-being of all citizens of the municipality, regardless of their ethnic background. What happened in the months that followed? Faced with the disastrous conditions caused by permanent shelling by enemy forces, faced with destroyed buildings, homes, houses, faced with destroyed building of medical centre, with bombed waterworks building, with lack of medicines, shortage of food, and other fundamental, basic needs, Dr. Simic and other municipal authorities worked on adoption of regulations with the aim to help everyone, regardless of their ethnic background. The Defence presented hundreds of exhibits and thousands of pages of witness testimonies regarding the scope and efforts of municipal authorities in Samac. Let me focus briefly on the Crisis Staff. You have heard the testimony, you have seen the legislation which outlines of legal competencies of the Crisis Staff, as well as the Municipal Assembly. You have also heard the testimonies of the witnesses who were able to shed light on the lack of authority, lack of control, the lack of effective power that the Crisis Staff had in general, and Dr. Simic had specifically. What did civilian municipal authorities have the power over? What were their competencies? Simply, they were empowered by the constitution, relevant laws, and the municipal statute of the following, inter alia: Number 1, economic development on the municipal level; urban development and communal housing, and communal housing; public and communal infrastructure; management of the state-owned apartments; communal activities of public interest; rental charges on the basis of rental policies at the republican level; adoption of municipal budget, and other areas, education, economy, and health care, being regulated by the republican level. We heard very extensive testimony and we have in our evidence these areas. Conversely, what they were not empowered, either by the law or by any other means, de jure or de facto, to impose their will or their way over the police - and specifically, I'm speaking now of the Prosecution's main witness, Mr. Todorovic - or the military. And I make reference to General Wilmot's report, because he outlined this issue in the chain of command of police of Republika Srpska, in chain of command of army of Republika Srpska. Of course, we shall disregard the other part of his testimony and his report related to events in Prijedor. We very well know why we introduced this expert report. So the relevant portions should be legislation relevant to police force in Republika Srpska and military in Republika Srpska, and we can find citation of certain laws which was at that time in force in General Wilmot's report. The Crisis Staff was not an exclusive authority above all other authorities. And Dr. Simic was not the omnipotent czar or even burgmeister or mayor, as the Prosecution has tendentiously but mistakenly been ascertaining throughout these proceedings. And while I do not want to get ahead of myself into discussing the role of Mr. Todorovic, whom the Prosecution has told us repeatedly to view with caution, for even they acknowledge in the tribunal of their own hearts and minds that he is less than honest, less than trustworthy, less than reliable raconteur of the truth. Even Mr. Todorovic during these few, fleeting moments of honesty and clarity admitted that he was a law unto himself, that he did as he willed. And, of course, the evidence bears out that he was running his own legal fiefdom in the toughest way, which only he was so heartfully able to do. Interestingly, we have available to us some jurisprudence from our sister Tribunal, the International Tribunal for Rwanda, which is quite relevant and pertinent to this case. I'm referring to the case Bagilishema, though it has been covered with some specificity in my brief, paragraphs 370 to 385. I invite your close scrutiny and attention as we reason through the situation in the case and the situation that we have before us. For the analogy or the comparison, it is remarkably significant and the Court's reasoning in Bagilishema case help us -- I will use some words, since I must skipper and pilot, so maybe to explain in some illustrative way. So the reasoning in Bagilishema case help us navigate through the fog of the Prosecution's argument. Because what I'm asking here, Madam President and Your Honours, is it to stay the course, to focus on what is the issue, to focus on what is the fact and belay straight through the Prosecution fanciful arguments. In Bagilishema, you have a burgmeister which is a mayor, which is equivalent to a mayor, and in that, unlike the situation in Bosanski Samac, the burgmeister who was the executive authority, had effective control and authority over the police. That authority was well recognised by the virtue of the existing legal framework, unlike in Bosanski Samac, where, as the evidence has shown, the police was under the authority of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. What is remarkable is that in that case, Bagilishema case, where, by law, it's burgmeister sits on the top of the police, gendarmerie, parapolice formations, and axiomatically enjoys command responsibility. So the Trial Chamber in Bagilishema acquitted Mr. Bagilishema and later the Appeals Chamber sitting here in The Hague confirmed the acquittal, having found that under the circumstances, that in spite of his legal authority, Bagilishema's legal authority, he did not have the means to detain or prevent activities that were being carried out in his commune. The evidence in this case, as I have indicated, shows that Dr. Simic exercised no authority over military police or other individuals within their chain of command. That Dr. Simic had no legal authority; that there were no means to contain those who were committing crimes; and more importantly, that Dr. Simic did what little he could do, which was to notify those who were in a command responsibility position to do something, to react, to contain, to stop, to remove, to prevent and to punish those who were committing crimes. Needless to draw your attention, Your Honours, to the issue of command responsibility, to the case-law, to the role of military commander within its zone of responsibility at this stage, and just a few words on the submission of Mr. Re during this morning, with regard to the - although we addressed that issue in our brief - with regard to the testimony of Mr. Paleksic, who was a member of commission. Let me clearly spell it out. That was internal affairs commission or department, like we know in Western systems of police, to investigate police misconduct. And Mr. Paleksic clearly testified that in this particular commission, the other members were in charge for some other area of investigation, including the certain acts of Mr. Todorovic. So it's an internal affairs commission of the republican Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. It was not some kind of informal commission where certain people are getting around. But the bottom line is that Dr. Simic was neither related to the army nor to the police. That's the bottom line. That's the core of our case. And finally, they admitted that by dismissing the count or charge 7(3), in earlier period, against Dr. Simic. Now, Your Honour, I will turn to the second part of my submission, the law and the evidence. First of all, the Prosecution did not plead its case with specific details in accordance with the principle that the accused right to know what is the case against him. I would now turn to address the issue of persecution, and then I will address the issue of catch-all charge of the concept of joint criminal enterprise; and finally, the issue of charges specified in the indictment. In fact, Your Honour, let me start with the concept of joint criminal enterprise. Now, in our written submission, we discussed in greater detail the applicable law in this case as it relates to fifth and final indictment and the arguments made by the Prosecution in this case. In its brief, however, the Prosecution invokes an allegation which is not contained in the indictment. I'm referring specifically to their usage of the allegation of joint criminal enterprise. In none of the five indictments had such term even been introduced. Surely this was not accidental. Surely this was not an oversight. Surely this was not unintentional. How can I speak with such assurance? No, Your Honours, I did not bug the Office of the Prosecutor to listen to their discussion in their sanctuary. No, I am not clairvoyant, and of course I was not a fly in the wall as the Prosecution sat around drafting and redrafting, conferring with their appellate lawyers as they formulated indictment after indictment after indictment, after indictment, after indictment, until they thought they had it right. Five amended indictments. Where they are with joint criminal enterprise? The Prosecution, in drafting its indictments, clearly, plainly, and unequivocally state, front and centre, that Prosecutors in this case, as we all know, do not have the authority to simply sit and draft the indictment and proceed without supervision and control. We all know that in fact these Prosecutors are supervised; in other words, they are subordinated to the more experienced Prosecutors, more seasoned Prosecutors, Prosecutors that have effective control and authority over them. And in this particular case, Your Honours, these Prosecutors, or should I say assistant Prosecutors or deputy Prosecutors, are supervised by none other than Mr. Peter McCloskey, a senior lawyer with the Office of the Prosecutor who of course in his faction, let us say, his common responsibility, oversaw the drafting of these indictments and who is a veteran of the usage of the concept joint criminal enterprise, this umbrella concept, this all embracing concept of joint criminal enterprise. Finally, needless to mention, also Madam Carla Del Ponte, well-known expert in pleading the concept of joint criminal enterprise. And we address this particular issue, analysing the work of the Office of the Prosecutor in our brief, listing the list of indictments where they use concept of joint criminal enterprise, plainly and blatantly. It is obvious that the concept of joint criminal enterprise is the spearhead and the heart of the work of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, at least in last four years. Yesterday, Mr. Re made a reference to the recent Appeals Chamber decision in Ojdanic case regarding the concept of joint criminal enterprise. Well, Mr. Re was wrong when he assumed that Dr. Simic's Defence was unaware of that decision. Our team worked very hardly, Mr. Re, and I can assure you that we worked diligently and profoundly and that we know very well what is the essence of this particular decision. And I can also assure Mr. Re that the Defence is of the opinion that it was not necessary, by the Defence to address this issue of joint criminal enterprise, due to the very simple reason: The concept of joint criminal enterprise was not pleaded in the indictment, and therefore it was useless to waste a limited size of our brief.
