However, reading Judge Hunt's separate opinion, since you raised that issue yesterday, it is clear that the expression "acting in concert together" was never mentioned. Perhaps Mr. Re was in hurry and was not even able to read properly the Honourable Judge Hunt's opinion, because in that opinion, there is no word of acting in concert together. Contrary to his submission, Honourable Judge Hunt made submission regarding the interchangeable usage of words "common purpose" and "joint criminal enterprise," which is rather different than the novel that we heard yesterday from Mr. Re. And yesterday again Mr. Re tried to explain the term "common purpose," which, according to his word, had shifted over the years. And then he stated that the process of shifting had culminated in the appeals decision in case of Ojdanic on 21st of May this year. And in his response to His Honour Judge Lindholm's question, this is at page 21 and 22 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Re was unable to make a reference to Tadic appeals decision, which was rendered on 15 of July, 1999. Mr. Re failed to mention that in the past four years his office had extensively been using the concept of joint criminal enterprise, four years, Your Honour. I shall not go into great detail, due to the time constraints. If he wishes, Mr. Re could also read two decisions dealing with joint criminal enterprise in the case of Brdjanin and Talic, which was rendered by the Honourable Judges Hunt, Mumba, and Liu. And finally, in response to Her Honour Judge Williams's question, page 27 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Re again introduced a novel in the Prosecution's submission by saying that, I quote: "I can't speak for those who drafted that aspect of indictment many years ago. All I can say is that the evidence is the same. And in the Prosecution's submission, it does not really matter." And then he concluded, Mr. Re concluded: "I am sorry, Your Honour Judge Williams. I just can't answer your question as to why it is pleaded that way." That was the word of my friend Mr. Re yesterday. These words clearly show that even the Prosecution does not know what they want to plead. So how the Defence may know what is the case to answer? It is also obvious that these Prosecutors in Samac case act in accordance with the proverb "la loi, c'est moi," since they do not have any relationship with their predecessors in this case, namely, Ms. Paterson and the other members of the -- at that time, because it's a quite longish case. In the light of the fact that these gentlemen have worked in concert together since April 2001, it is defies belief that even today Mr. Re does not know what the Prosecution case is about. The Defence, in its paragraph 659 of its brief provided an extensive list of the indictments filed by the Office of the Prosecutor where the concept of joint criminal enterprise is clearly and loudly pleaded, yet this indictment, this fifth indictment, which is the manifestation of four previous indictments, does not contain the common purpose concept. This clearly could not be an oversight, no more so than it could have been an oversight than Bosanski Samac municipality was struck out from the crown case of the Office of the Prosecutor, and that is the case Krajisnik and Plavsic. There is no Bosanski Samac municipality in Plavsic and Krajisnik case. And in addition, Your Honours, two co-defendants in this case, namely, Mr. Milan Simic and Mr. Stevan Todorovic, reached the agreement with the Prosecution and consequently plea bargain agreements were signed. Your Honour, it is a well-known fact that in these agreements, there is no single letter with regard to the concept of joint criminal enterprise. What conclusions we may draw from the above-mentioned facts? Number one: The Prosecution decided not to include Bosanski Samac municipality in the Krajisnik and Plavsic case due to the simple and obvious fact, there is no relationship between the top political leadership of Republika Srpska and municipal civilian authorities in Bosanski Samac with regard to the alleged common purpose. Number 2: The Prosecution failed to plead with sufficient precision the concept of joint criminal enterprise in this case, and therefore it was not included in plea bargain agreement of the former co-defendants Mr. Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic in this case. And number 3: It is perfectly clear that the policy of the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to Bosanski Samac case does not support the attempt of these gentlemen to introduce, out of the blue, on a last-minute basis, the concept of joint criminal enterprise in this particular case. The superior commanders of these associate Prosecutors consciously, carefully, and after considerable and repeated deliberation, and I say this because, after all, we do have five indictments, specifically refrained not to include this all-encompassing charge of joint criminal enterprise, which seems to be the flavour of the day for the Prosecution in charging the accused that come before this Tribunal. The Prosecution now, after the close of the evidence, and after Dr. Simic has exhausted his possibilities for presenting his defence, now, yesterday, now they raise the concept of joint criminal enterprise. It is almost Kafkaesque and by that I mean that Dr. Simic has been deprived of his fair trial rights guaranteed under the Statute and in particular of knowing what he is supposed to defend himself against. The Prosecution has an obligation to draft an indictment with a certain degree of specificity that would allow any accused, number one, to know exactly what he has been charged of; number two, what the Prosecution will be required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt; and number three, what he will need to defend against. In this case, the Prosecution argues that Dr. Simic was involved in a joint criminal enterprise. If we are to believe the Prosecution, if we are to accept their argument, if we are to permit them to advance this theory at this stage, we would have to accept and conclude that there was a massive conspiracy that started with the creation of Republika Srpska, in pursuit of the aspiration for self-determination by the Bosnian Serb, which in fact was a natural and conceivable consequence under the circumstances, particularly when those exact sentiments were shared by the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims. First, this Trial Chamber should disallow any argument made by the Prosecution, be it in written submission or the oral submission, with respect to the concept of joint criminal enterprise. It was not pleaded, and therefore, it should not be argued. The crux of the Prosecution argument, if I am to understand what exactly they were attempting to convey, is that, in a very surreptitious manner, they now wish it allege and argue that they have proved that the Crisis Staff itself, as an institution, was none other than a joint criminal enterprise which was a part of a larger joint criminal enterprise and that Dr. Simic was the leader, at least in Bosanski Samac, of this joint criminal enterprise, and as such, should be held responsible for anything and everything that might have occurred in Bosanski Samac during the period of the indictment. Nowhere in the indictment does it state that the Crisis Staff was a joint criminal enterprise. Nowhere in the indictment does it state that Dr. Simic was a part of the joint criminal enterprise. Nowhere in the indictment does the phrase or the concept or the notion of joint criminal enterprise appear, yet now, at this stage of proceedings, after the evidence has been closed, the Prosecution wishes to argue for something that they never alleged, and, as I have noted earlier, it is not by coincidence that it was never alleged, and I submit that not being able to come through the front door, now they are trying to sneak in, not through the back but through the basement window. Since the Prosecution has failed to properly plead the concept of joint criminal enterprise, this Honourable Trial Chamber should reject its submission with that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: What, in your submission, do the words "acting in concert together" mean?, acting in concert together, the three accused persons, and with other Serb civilian and military officials? I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It means nothing for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We need to know what in your submission, how we are to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, it means nothing to me, because the wording of the indictment with that regard is absolutely vague, imprecise, and I'll quote, count number 1, paragraph 11 of the indictment: "Acting in concert together, and with other Serb civilian and military officials." This vagueness and imprecision in these words brings me to the conclusion that this word means nothing to me. And certainly, these words means no joint criminal enterprise, no common purpose, no common concept. Because we all know, within the case-law of this Tribunal, what these particular concepts are. And certainly, Your Honour, in five amended indictments, we didn't hear that. But this is a legal argument. That's my position. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for elaborating on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're welcome. In terms of persecution, I would like now to move on to the charge of persecution and briefly discuss the matter. I will not go into the technical/legal aspects given in our written submission we have addressed that. But I would like to focus the Trial Chamber to the facts as they have come before this Trial Chamber, for this these acts are considered in their specific scope and context the inevitable truth that emerges is that Dr. Simic was not involved in any acts that would fall under this umbrella charge of persecution that is charged in the indictment, catch-all charge. I have already discussed during my remarks on the historical context of the events preceding to the establishment of the Crisis Staff, and I have outlined Dr. Simic's role in the community of him being a duly elected official prior to the outbreak of the war, the lawful establishment of the Crisis Staff, and the limited but legitimate and lawful competencies of the Crisis Staff and of Dr. Simic in particular. And therefore, in my respectful submission, that Dr. Simic did not plan, instigate, order, commit, or otherwise aided and abetted a forcible takeover of Bosanski Samac. Dr. Simic and the evidence is very clear, was not responsible under any of the modalities as I have indicated in our brief and which are pleaded in the catch-all form in the indictment, namely, in arresting, detaining, confining, or deploying non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, nor he is responsible for any cruel or inhumane treatment of any non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac. He did not forcibly transfer or expel anyone from Bosanski Samac. In short, at no time did he directly or indirectly do any of the enumerated acts outlined in count 1 of the indictment. The evidence demonstrates, for instance, when it comes to the deportation and expulsion or forcible transfer, that many people left Bosanski Samac, not only non-Serbs, but Serbs as well, and humanitarian problem was in place to allow those who wished to leave, could do so, and all those who wished to stay could stay. That's the case of Bosanski Samac. We heard from 30-some witnesses who indicated that while they wanted to stay, they felt compelled to leave because they were insecure of their safety and their future in Bosanski Samac. Obviously, Your Honours, you must all take into consideration the conditions at that time, which for everyone in that community were simply uncertain and uncomfortable. There was a war, daily shelling, municipality on the first metre of front line on the bank of Sava River. Enemy forces shelled Bosanski Samac every day. The shell is not smart shell like we have now in certain military actions. In 1992, shell was ordinary and the shell did not choose who to kill or to wound or what to destroy. That was the life in Samac at that time. However, I submit that in weighing this evidence, you must also counterbalance it with the testimonies of 30-some witnesses presented by the Defence. When the non-Serbs got to the line to cross over, in accordance with their wish, they chose on their own to remain. They choose to remain voluntarily, not by threat. They were certainly not pushed over line, since they were right there, which is what you would expect if the intent was to ethnically cleanse, get rid of, eradicate their presence, but instead they were welcomed back into the community, where contrary to the fears expressed by the witnesses for the Prosecution, these witnesses, Defence witnesses, non-Serb, they were able to stay in their homes, life, within their communities and safely remain members of the Bosanski Samac community, which is of course a testament that there was no plan to ethnically cleanse, and also we must keep in mind the evidence that were heard that Serbs were leaving also. Is this also part of the Prosecution argument of persecution? Were the Serbs, municipal authorities, or Dr. Simic attempting to ethnically cleanse Bosanski Samac of Serbs as well? And so I submit that when you look at all of the evidence, when you look at the conditions in Bosanski Samac at the time, when you look at the movement of the peoples to and from Bosanski Samac, when you look at the voluntariness of those who wished to leave and those who wished to stay, when you look at what happened to those who stayed, the only inevitable conclusion that can be drawn is that the Prosecution has failed to meet its burden of proof of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Dr. Simic was involved in any of the alleged activities contained in the indictment. The Prosecution has specifically failed in establishing the requisite but indispensable element of mens rea, that is, the discriminatory nature of the acts. What do we know in this particular case? We know that in carrying out his functions that were prescribed to him by law in his capacity as a speaker of the Crisis Staff, he carried out his duties in a non-discriminatory fashion, as I noted earlier, with regard to his specific competencies, he provided food, medical assistance, aid, to all citizens, irrespective of their ethnic background or religious beliefs. Was there discrimination on the ground in Bosanski Samac at that time? Were certain members of the community targeted, abused? The answer is yes. Was Dr. Simic responsible for that activity? No. Although the Defence in its brief has submitted its view with regarding the charges and the objective elements of the crimes charged in article 5(H) and 5(D), and Article 2 of the Statute, please allow me to address very briefly the following issues. Number 1: The Prosecution failed to plead the international armed conflict issue in its indictment. There is no word of the nature of the conflict in its indictment. Knowing that the nature of the conflict is a requisite objective element for application of Article 2 of the Statute, the conclusion is that this count should be dismissed. For this reason and for the reason of the submission the Defence made in its brief and throughout the proceedings. Number 2: The Prosecution failed to plead the specific armed conflict between Croatia and FR Yugoslavia, and another novel of Mr. Re yesterday, he informed us here, after all these years of proceedings - it's page 51 and 52 - that in fact Prosecution, that's for the first time since 1995, it's almost ten years, that the Prosecution actually, speaking about the international conflict between state of Croatia and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. No Bosnia at all. We agree with Mr. Re, because, number 1, we think that Bosnia at that time was never a state in terms of international law, only after Dayton; and number 2, that the legitimate -- a legitimate request of Bosnian Serbs made through the plebiscite in October 1991 showed that they were -- actually exercised their right for self-determination and wanted to be a part of the other state subject. Only yesterday we heard another novel that the two states were fighting in the municipality of Samac, as I stated, Croatia and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Defence is confused, since Mr. Re did not mention the other aspects of his case, and I submit that maybe the reason is that -- the reasons provided by the Defence were so convincible, so that actually he agrees that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not at that time a state. Although Mr. Re is not obliged to read the Defence brief, I'm referring to paragraphs 392 to 430. He should be aware of the findings in paragraph 77 of Tadic decision on the Defence motion on jurisdiction. He should also be aware of the fact that the case-law of this Tribunal directs that each case should be viewed separately, which means that the issue of the existence of international armed conflict in Samac case should be decided based on the evidence of this particular case, and the burden of proof is on the Prosecution. Also the Prosecution should be aware of the ruling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just before you move on, again I'd like to hear a submission or two on interpreting page 3 of the fifth amended indictment, entitled "general legal allegations." I'm particularly interested in paragraph number 6 and paragraph number 7, and with respect to paragraph number 6, at all times relevant to this indictment, a state of armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." I know it says a state of armed conflict. It doesn't say international or internal. But it does say "and partial occupation." So I'd be interested in hearing your interpretation of armed conflict and partial occupation, what they mean, and then tie it in with number 7, which says: "All of the persons described in the indictment as victims were protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949." If you would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Since the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in process of dissolution, state of armed conflict existed, and the partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was occupied by at least three entities: Muslim-led government, so-called central government, because we heard, Your Honours, from the Prosecution witness Mr. Tihic, Sulejman Tihic. Now he's a head of state. He's head of state of Bosnia. Throughout 1992 and 1993, the Muslim-led government controlled even less than 20 and 30 per cent of whole territory. The other entity was Bosnian Croats. They controlled 30 to 40. And the third was Bosnian Serb side, also controlling, depending on the time, between 40 and 60 per cent of the territory. And finally by Dayton Peace Accord they were allowed to have 49 per cent. In my respectful submission the state of armed conflict was in territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was internal armed conflict. And yes, it was a partial occupation by three warring sides in Bosnia. In order to follow the principles what must be pleaded in indictment, we have also clearly to say: When you want to use Article 2, dear gentlemen, you have to exactly plead that it was the nature of conflict, because this is a requisite objective element of the Article 2. And yes, Your Honour, in response to your second question, yes, in paragraph 7, at all times relevant to the indictment, the -- all persons were protected by Geneva Conventions of 1949. Yes. Not only Geneva Conventions. I may say in broader terms the concept of international humanitarian law. We do not have to stick specifically to certain articles. This is the rule of the game. This is the role of the Prosecution, to plead exact article. But from my respectful submission, Your Honour, I think that the notion of international humanitarian law should be viewed in the broader context, including the protocols of Geneva Conventions and many, many others, other sources. So in this particular case, yes, they were protected by Geneva Conventions, but it was not a case that Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions can be applied, as pleaded by the Prosecution. Because in order to do so, they have to prove, first of all, to plead with certain certainty in the indictment this fact, and then to prove the exhibits. They failed to do so, Your Honours. As I said, even one of their key witnesses, head of the state, Mr. Tihic, a diplomat, jurist, expert in law, he stated that actually Muslim-led central government was not in control of more than 20 or 30 per cent of the territory, which is absolutely a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one follow-up. So if I hear you correctly, and I think I have, partial occupation, in your submission, was just between the three ethnic or national communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In your submission, there was no occupation by persons or forces from outside of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Specifically, if we are speaking according to the principles of the case-law within this Tribunal, we are specifically speaking about Bosanski Samac municipality, that territory. I'm not entering into the area of the other -- into the nature of conflict in the other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the position of Defence is that in Bosanski Samac municipality, there was not an intervention or, so to say, occupation of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And last question on the same note: We've heard a lot, of course, about the Specials, volunteers, paramilitaries, whatever one wants to call them, coming into the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Could their presence be viewed as partial occupation and hence internationalising the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that would be really, from my respectful submission, that would be really very hard to conclude, because we heard the evidence that this group of 15 or 20 volunteers or, call them whatever anyone like, was a part of the larger unit, firstly, 17th Tactical Group, of 7.000 soldiers, and then of 2nd Posavina Brigade, which is maybe four or five thousand soldiers, whereas they were members of special battalion, consisting, Your Honours - you know that very well from the evidence - consisting of around 400 or 500 local villagemen, local young boys living in the area. So if one wants to conclude that 15 or 20 persons coming on their voluntary basis like in Spanish civil war or maybe, you know, in war in Afghanistan or now in Iraq, which is absolutely other issue, if these 15 or 20 among the thousands of local soldiers, local young boys and fathers and grandfathers and brothers, fighting for their houses, for their homes, if someone will, from this fact, because they are coming -- we even don't have evidence from where they came. Many -- a few of them, but we don't know. Maybe they were born in Bosnia. What is the reason, et cetera. We don't have evidence, Your Honour, in our particular case, whether they were under certain control of someone, superior, on behalf they acted. Because as far as we know in this case, they were members of the local units, where majority was local population. So the attempt to magnify this case by the Prosecution, Your Honour, inevitably draws us to very uncertain legal area. This is my submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So as I said, also going back to the issue expressed in our brief with regard to this objective element of Article 2, the Prosecution should be aware of the ruling in this particular case of 4th of April, 2003, where this Honourable Trial Chamber stated that it was, I quote, "inaccurate that the Prosecution had introduced three expert witness testimonies dealing with the nature of the conflict through Rule 92 bis." At this point, the Defence would like to emphasise that in spite of its objection, the pre-trial Chamber ruled in favour of Prosecution motion. Because during pre-trial phase, we, objecting to the -- for the way that Prosecution will make introduction of these 92 bis statements, but our motion was rejected. And that was the reason why the Defence had tried to introduce its own military expert report, in terms of the concept of nature of the conflict, and certain relations between army of Republika Srpska, JNA, and some other units in the area, simply in order to challenge the Prosecution's submission regarding the nature of the conflict, being one of the elements for the application of Article 2 of the Statute. And yesterday Mr. Re invited this Trial Chamber to take judicial notice as to the nature of the armed conflict, page 53. Again, Defence would like to remind Mr. Re that the Prosecution failed in this attempt during the pre-trial phase. He is a freshman here. Maybe he's not aware about it. I advised Mr. Re to familiarise himself of the earlier stage of proceedings of this case. We have a ruling in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, there is no need for you to address Mr. Re like that. You simply go on as to what the evidence is all about and how you interpret it; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that. With regard to the issue of statehood, the Defence reiterates its position stated in Defence brief. The basis of the Defence submission can be found, inter alia, in statement of top-ranking official of Australian ministry of foreign affairs, Mr. Ronald Rich who stated in Bosnia-Herzegovina's admission to the UN, "the UN Security Council had unanimously recommended this country's membership and the General Assembly had unanimously accepted the recommendation. Yet every newspaper reader in the world knew by that time that not only could Bosnia and Herzegovina not be accurately described as independent, but it could hardly be described as a state." These words speak for themselves. Given the fact that the Prosecution failed to prove the objective elements of Article 2 of the Statute, count 3 to the indictment, should be dismissed. With regard to the cumulative charge in count 1 and 2 of the indictment, in the light of the fact that both counts encompass same objective elements required for the application of Article 5 of the Statute, the Defence is convinced that this Trial Chamber will make proper ruling on that issue at a later stage. Also, I am compelled to argue and to hope that in viewing the facts in this case you will view them as they specifically relate to Dr. Simic and specifically hold the Prosecution in demonstrating each and every element, such as, for instance, the element of mens rea, and that these -- the Prosecution arguments will not be accepted. In fact, with regard to Dr. Simic's mens rea, Dr. Simic was not behind of the process described as ethnic cleansing, as stated by the Prosecution. Dr. Simic was not part of it. Dr. Simic was never expressed his mens rea, the requisite element for the application of the Article 5 of -- actually, crime of persecution is the specific higher level of mens rea, which is the intent to discriminate or to act on discriminatory basis. Your Honours, the overwhelming evidence in this case clearly establishes the state of mind of Dr. Simic. Dr. Simic wholeheartedly participated in all activities of civilian municipal authorities in order to improve living conditions of thousands of citizens of Bosanski Samac municipality, as I earlier stated, municipality situated at the front line, a community suffering of daily shelling, and society suffering from lack of food, medications, water, and electricity. He did so without any discriminatory intent and for the benefit of all members of society, regardless of their ethnic background. So the evidence clearly shows that Dr. Simic did not possess a requisite state of mind in order to be held responsible for the crime of persecution, as charged in count 1 of the indictment. With regard to the Prosecution claims from -- submitted in their brief, the -- in para 1, Prosecution claims that the Crisis Staff and its military assistants ethnically cleansed an entire municipality of its Croats and Muslims. The Defence respectfully submits and includes by reference all its prior submissions and pleadings that there was no ethnic cleansing in Bosanski Samac municipality, that all non-Serbs who lived in the part of pre-war municipality of Samac, namely, in Domaljevac, in surrounding area - this is the other part of the pre-war municipality of Samac - lived there before the outbreak of hostilities, during the civil war in Bosnia, and even after the Dayton Peace Accord. So there is no evidence or any grounds to say that Dr. Simic could ethnically cleanse someone who was living there before the war, during the war, and after the Dayton. I'm specifically addressing this issue with regard to the Croat-controlled part of pre-war municipality of Bosanski Samac, which now and during the war was named as Bosanski Samac Domaljevac, and we heard many overwhelming evidence with that regard, but I believe that my learned friend Mr. Lukic will address this issue in more detail, with regard to the demographic issues. So the Prosecution failed to provide evidence regarding the allegation of ethnic cleansing in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. With regard to the Prosecution's submissions in chapter 2 of its brief, it is clear that the Prosecution, by alleging the concept of joint criminal enterprise tried to fabricate impossible theory regarding participation of an accused in all three types of joint criminal enterprise. This is another novel of Prosecution. This legal novel is by all means an unfounded allegation without any reference to the case-law of the Tribunal, and the Defence has already addressed this issue in the earlier part of this submission. With regard to the allegations of the existence of an overall joint criminal enterprise in Republika Srpska, it is clear from the Defence's previous submission that this is an ill-founded theory. The Prosecution referenced in its paragraph 22 of its brief regarding the work of so-called - I'm quoting - "constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina" is totally groundless, due to the fact that it is obvious that none of the Bosnia and Herzegovina institutions led by Muslims, Bosnian Muslims, at that time, did not express and they were not legitimate acting on behalf of all three constituent nations. They acted on behalf of only Bosnian Muslims. That was a period of dissolution of the state, and, as stated in our earlier submission, and as stated by the Defence expert, Professor Pavle Nikolic. In addition, the Defence respectfully submits that it is clear from the evidence that SAO Northern Bosnia never operated and therefore it is impossible to infer or to conclude -- to make any relevant conclusion regarding the existence of such a body, when one body is not existing, there is not any consequences of the work of non-existing body. With regard to the Prosecution's submission on the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the period between September 1991 and mid-April 1992, the Defence reiterates its position stated in its brief and throughout the trial proceedings, and I, with some details this morning, explained what is the position of the Defence with regard to the certain events in period of September 1991, as pleaded in the indictment, until the April of 1992. With regard to paragraph 35 of the Prosecution brief, the Defence reiterates its position that the words "state borders" are inaccurately translated from B/C/S, since the right meaning of the word -- I will say that in B/C/S, r-a-z-g-r-a-n-i-c-e-n-j-e, should read as delineation, delineation. As translated by the official court interpreters. And we could find this translation in transcript 12590. In relation to paragraph 36, the Defence submits that the quotation made by the Prosecution is irrelevant to this case, since President Radovan Karadzic, in his words, at 50th session of Republika Srpska assembly held on 5th and 6th of April, 1995, did not mention Bosanski Samac municipality by any word. So it's irrelevant. In paragraph 38 of its brief, the Prosecution probably unintentionally increased the percentage of the electorate to 64 per cent. In fact, the exact figure was and should be 63.4 per cent. In any case, it was less than two-thirds of total voting population. In the same paragraph, the Prosecution uses the term "Bosnian government" in relation to the international recognition. As stated by the Defence, this word should be read, according to the Defence understanding, as "Muslim-led Bosnian government," and this fact negates the legitimacy of the process of recognition. Probably by omission, although I think that my colleague changed that yesterday, but I must quote, because in Prosecution brief, in para 4-0, mentioned two dates, 29th of April, 1992, when allegedly Serbian Montenegro themself proclaimed to be successors of the SFRY, and 19 of May, 1992, as the date when Bosnia-Herzegovina was admitted as a state member to UN. I believe that it was corrected in yesterday's submission, but for the record, since I'm analysing Prosecution brief. Then in paragraph 42 of its brief, the Prosecution states that the Serb forces attacked and took over 11 towns in northern Bosnia, listing, among others, towns of Bijeljina, Zvornik, and Foca. For the sake of clarity, the Defence would like to respectfully bring to this Trial Chamber's attention a well-known fact that none of these towns are locate in northern Bosnia. With regard to the paragraph 45, and specifically, footnote 66, it is obvious that the Prosecution misinterpreted the evidence. The Defence respectfully states that the Defence Exhibit D166/1 clearly shows that the SDS in Bosanski Samac did not form any military units within the municipality. In addition, none of the witnesses mentioned in footnote 66 corroborates this Prosecution assertation with regard to reference in paragraph 47, the Defence states that Maksim Simeunovic in his capacity as intelligence officer of 17th Tactical Group, like the other military witnesses, desperately tried to minimise his personal role and the role of the 17th Tactical Group in military operations conducted within the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Furthermore, the Prosecution relies on Simo Zaric's testimony in paragraph 48 of its brief, but the exact words of Mr. Zaric, such as, and I'm quoting: "You could." And then another word, I'm quoting: "This is my conviction." And I'm quoting again: "This is my opinion." So these words clearly shows that, number one, Simo Zaric only speculate in his statement; and number 2, that Simo Zaric, as the other military officials, tried to minimise the role of military in the events in Bosanski Samac; number 3, since Mr. Zaric is speaking of the so-called shadow government, it is obvious that he is neither a constitutional law expert, nor he's an international law expert, so he cannot be able to give evidence, reliable evidence, regarding these issues. And it is rather strange that the Prosecution did not rely on someone else who might be of better assistance with regard to these issues. As regards paragraph 49, the Prosecution misinterpreted words of Defence witness Savo Popovic, because Mr. Popovic clearly stated that the Crisis Staff did not take part in taking over the territory of Odzak, number 1; number 2, that he doesn't know about the killings and that there are certain similarities between Milan Simic and Biljana Plavsic's statements, but only these similarities are in wording and not in factual basis regarding the actual situation in Odzak. So getting out of context a few words doesn't mean that it is the evidence. So these portions should be viewed in the totality of the testimony of Mr. Savo Popovic. Then the Prosecution referenced to the testimony of Marko Tubakovic, commander of 2nd Detachment of 17th Tactical Group, as stated in its paragraph 50, is clear example of misunderstanding and misinterpretation of evidence. Marko Tubakovic clearly stated that volunteers who arrived in Samac intimated [sic] all citizens. Since it is indisputable that Lugar group was under command of the military and since Marko Tubakovic was the commander of the 2nd Detachment and later member of the command of 2nd Posavina Brigade, it is clear that he and the other officers were solely responsible for the acts of the members of Lugar group. This is a concept of command responsibility. In addition, Tubakovic testified that nowhere in the platform of the SDS party the issue of ethnic intolerance was stated. That was the word of Marko Tubakovic. With regard to paragraph 58 to 61 of the Prosecution brief, which relate to the alleged role of Dr. Simic in the alleged joint criminal enterprise, the Defence reiterates and includes by reference its position and roles the attention of the Honourable Trial Chamber that is clear from the evidence in this trial that Dr. Simic did not play any role in the appointment of military commanders and that this process was in the hands of Superior Command, namely, the 17th Corps of JNA and later Eastern Bosnia Corps of VRS. With regard to the alleged consultation with Frenki Simatovic, shall we go -- the Defence relies on the Exhibits under the -- shall we go in private? No? Shall we go in private?

utterances.text: Are you discussing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we go in private for a second, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution relies heavily on so-called variant A and B, Exhibit P3 and P45, instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a state of emergency, to establish a connection between the actions of Bosnia -- Bosnian Serb leadership and the municipal authorities in Bosanski Samac. We addressed that issue in our paragraphs 26, 32, and 108 in more details in our brief. However, yesterday Mr. Re stated that the Prosecution of course acknowledges that it does not have a copy that was sent to Bosanski Samac. Yes, the Defence agrees with the Prosecution due to the simple fact that this particular document does not exist at all, and that is why it cannot be ascribed to the municipal authorities in Bosanski Samac. The reference of the Prosecution with regard to the other municipalities is absolutely irrelevant to this case. We don't have evidence in this case regarding that particular document. In its final trial brief, the Defence addresses this document in the paragraphs 207, 561, 648, and in its discussion of the Exhibit P3 on page of Defence brief 136 and elsewhere in the brief. Briefly, this document, this exhibit, P3 or P45, as you wish, this is an unauthenticated document that was never even discussed by the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac, as testified by several members of the civilian municipal authorities in Samac. This document did not bear the customary stamp or signature and the highest organ of Republika Srpska SDS denied its existence. In our submission, we make the reference to the Defence exhibits to that extent. Further, there is no direct evidence showing that the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff was created pursuant to this document. As evidence of a plan for the forcible takeover, the Prosecution notes that several other Crisis Staffs were formed elsewhere in B and H after the alleged issuance in December of 1991. However, the Samac Crisis Staff was not created until five months later, namely, on 19 of April, 1992. And in response to an impending attack by Croat and Muslim forces on Bosanski Samac. And again, I reiterate my submission with regard to the joint criminal enterprise which was alleged in Krajisnik and Plavsic case, covering dozens of municipalities of Republika Srpska, and then it was struck out. And this issue raised an obvious question: Why did the OTP remove Bosanski Samac from its allegation of a joint criminal enterprise in that particular case? The Defence respectfully submits that the reason for this is because there was in fact no joint criminal enterprise among the civilian authorities of Bosanski Samac. Further, there is no evidence to indicate a link or a nexus between the top leadership of Republika Srpska and the municipal authorities of Bosanski Samac with regard to the alleged crime of persecution. Then the Prosecution cites, in para 109, a meeting in village of Struke, in Odzak municipality, on 29 of February, 1992. I would like to address the issue of the chronology of the Prosecution, because obviously there is discrepancy between the date to this particular -- related to this particular meeting in Struke. It's actually 29 February and 29 March. So it is not accurate in submission of the Prosecution. Because in paragraph 109, the Prosecution uses period 29 February and in chronology it's 29 March. So it's ambiguous. The Prosecution alleges that the meeting was held in Struke, at which Dr. Simic allegedly stated that the JNA would protect the Serb population and that the Serbian municipality of Samac had been formed earlier that day. The Prosecution relies solely on the evidence provided by its witness Blaz Paradzik. However, Dr. Simic denied making any such statement or speech at this meeting, or that he even saw Mr. Paradzik at that meeting. And further, Defence witness Mitar Nijemcevic, the owner of the house in Struke where the meeting was held, although with the other agenda, testified that Dr. Simic was merely passing through the village and state only for a few minutes and gave no speeches. The same witness testified that Paradzik was not present at the meeting. Thus, the only reasonable conclusion is that the Paradzik testimony holds no weight and the testimony of Dr. Simic and the owner of the house, Mr. Nijemcevic, should be believed. And as I said, we addressed that matter in our brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Before I -- beginning with this second part of my submission -- I mean the other part of my submission, just a small correction to the transcript. It is page 69, line 5. Instead of word "intimated" should be "intimidated." In correction to the transcript, page 65, line 5, instead of word "intimated" should be "intimidated." The Prosecution states in its paragraph 110 that the Serb assembly of Bosanski Samac on 28th March 1992 elected officials who would later run the "post coup organs of government." The bare fact is that the Prosecution failed to present any evidence that the officials at the meeting acted with a post coup or parallel government in mind or acted in furtherance of so-called variant A and B. In fact, Bogdanovic was not even a member of the SDS at that time, as testified by Todorovic, transcript 9048. And Todorovic had previously been thrown out of the party after the 1990 municipal elections of Samac municipality, as testified by Dr. Simic, transcript 12236. Further, a list of officials elected at that meeting clearly shows that several persons elected at that time were not members of any party or were members of other parties. In addition, there is no evidence that the elected members of the municipal Executive Board were all members of SDS. Therefore, it is simply untenable to hold that the mere election of some officials belonging to the SDS party, along with the officials from other parties, must have been conducted pursuant to so-called variant A and B. At any rate, the Prosecution claims on this issue are groundless is supported by the fact that the Prosecution failed to elicit any evidence that the acts of Todorovic and Bogdanovic were committed in furtherance of so-called variant A and B document. Lastly, there is no evidence to indicate that Dr. Simic, who was not a speaker of the Municipal Assembly at that time, that was Ilija Ristic, and later on acting president Dusan Tanasic as we know from the Exhibit P124. So Dr. Simic -- there's no evidence that Dr. Simic played any significant role in these elections or acted in any way to further the so-called variant A and B. In essence, the Prosecution seeks to portray the valid election of municipal officials as a crime. In addition, the Prosecution alleges that a small but trusted SDS welcoming committee met paramilitaries in Batkusa, paragraph 113. It is reckless for the Prosecution to insinuate that the mere presence of Todorovic and Ivanovic in Batkusa constitutes an SDS welcoming committee. In this situation, both men were likely acting in their capacity as military officials, as testified by Todorovic, transcript 9038. In brief, there is no evidence that they were sent by the SDS as an organisation or by Dr. Simic personally to this meeting. Following the Prosecution logic, it would seem that any time two people who happened to be members of the same party gather at the meeting, it constitutes official party action. Further, following the Prosecution reasoning, it is more reasonable inference, given the fact that these two men acted on behalf of the military. The Lugar group was under the command and control of the 17th Tactical Group. As such, their presence in the area of Bosanski Samac municipality was clearly a military operation, a part of military operation. Ivanovic was a commander with the 1st Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group, as stated in Prosecution brief paragraph 113, and Todorovic was assistant commander for intelligence of the 1st detachment of the 17th Tactical Group. And moreover, Maksim Simeunovic, who was at that time assistant commander for intelligence of 17th Tactical Group, testified that, I'm quoting, "an associate called him to inform him of the arrival of the Lugar group in Batkusa," transcript 15856. Simeunovic further testified that in the course of verifying the arrival of the Lugar group, he went to the 1st detachment in Batkusa, where he saw both Ivanovic and Todorovic standing outside. In order to logically establish a connection between the SDS and the actions of Todorovic and Ivanovic, the Prosecution is required to show some form of active direction on the part of SDS or Dr. Simic. And they failed to do so. On the contrary, the evidence overwhelmingly indicates that the arrival of the Lugar group was solely a military operation; indeed, this is another example of the Prosecution making unfounded inferential leaps based on evidence that does not support the Prosecution's conclusions. In paragraph 114, the Prosecution alleges that Dr. Simic was present at meeting on Donji Zabar on 12th of April, 1992, with military officials, indicating Dr. Simic's participation in the so-called takeover. Again, the Prosecution appears to contradict itself. Elsewhere in its brief, the Prosecution seeks to portray Dr. Simic as having authority and control over police and military affairs in Samac. However, in this section, the Prosecution acknowledges that the JNA and not the civilian authorities transported the Lugar group to Batkusa. Further, the Prosecution concedes that Colonel Nikolic not Dr. Simic or any other civilian official arranged this meeting. Moreover, Dr. Simic denied being present at this meeting. But even assuming Dr. Simic was at that meeting, Colonel Nikolic himself testified that all of the present at the meeting did so at his express invitation, so that he could ascertain the identity of the Lugar group and the reasons for their presence and to discuss the situation in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Thus, it is clear the purpose of the meeting was to gather information on activities occurring in Bosanski Samac, not to formulate plans for takeover. Colonel Nikolic further testified that no plans for cooperation between military and the SDS were discussed or formed at this meeting. Moreover, Nikolic testified that Stevan Todorovic did most of the talking, and admitted at that meeting that he, rather than Dr. Simic, played a significant role in the arrival of the Lugar group. In light of the foregoing, it is clear that the Prosecution failed to prove Dr. Simic's active participation in the planning of takeover, beyond a reasonable doubt. The alleged mere presence of the accused at this meeting is not sufficient to establish individual criminal responsibility under the international law. Certainly, there is no evidence Dr. Simic advocated joint action between JNA and SDS for a forcible takeover. In paragraph 115, the Prosecution cites a meeting between the SDA, SDS, and HDZ on or around 13th of April, 1992, in the municipal building where Dr. Simic allegedly issued an ultimatum. The Defence addressed this issue in its brief in paragraphs 253, 254, and 600. Dr. Simic denied making any ultimatums or threats and testified that the purpose of the meeting was to discuss the implementation of the conclusions of international community, inter alia, Lisbon agreement and the situation in the region. Furthermore, several witnesses present at that meeting testified that the atmosphere was generally calm and tolerant and that Dr. Simic did not make any ultimatums or threatening comments. Moreover, Dusan Tanasic, the acting speaker of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Samac and Pelagicevo also testified that the meeting was generally calm and Dr. Simic did not make any threatening comments. In fact, Defence witness Simeon Simic, being present at that meeting, testified that one exception to this was when Izet Izetbegovic, the Prosecution witness, one of the leaders of the local chapter of the SDA [Realtime transcript read in error "SDS"] party, continued to make threatening comments such as, I'm quoting: "You have your own army. I have mine, and that is how we will resolve this." Transcript 13000. There's just a correction, sorry, to the transcript, page 77, line 14, instead of SDS party, should be SDA. In addition, the only evidence the Prosecution cites in attributing these comments to Dr. Simic is testimony of Sulejman Tihic, and Izetbegovic both members of the opposition SDA party. In contrast, several witnesses from various parties at that meeting testified that Dr. Simic uttered what became a well-known statement. I'm quoting: "It is better to negotiate for hundred days than to go to war for even a single day." Several witnesses confirmed that Dr. Simic added: "There is no state which is worth shedding a child's tear, let alone a drop of child's blood." Transcript 12999. Furthermore, Defence witness Simeon Simic testified that the meeting was chaired by Mato Nujic, a Croat, who was an HDZ representative and a speaker of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac. At that meeting, Mr. Nujic informed those at the meeting of the establishment of the Croatian community of Bosnian Posavina and that the municipality of Bosanski Samac was included in this territory. In addition, he raised the issue of the partition of the territory, referring to international documents, transcript 12994-13000. In sum, at least four witnesses from various parties testified that Dr. Simic was calm and tolerant during this meeting and in fact implored those gathered to seek a peaceful solution. The Prosecution could cite only two members of the SDA, political opponents of Dr. Simic, who alleged that Dr. Simic made a threatening comment. Additionally, a witness present at that meeting testified that it was a Croat representative who chaired the meeting and raised the issue of partition of the territory. Thus, it is clear that the Prosecution failed to meet its burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Dr. Simic made these alleged comments. In paragraph 116, the Prosecution cites the Samac Official Gazette in alleging that the Crisis Staff was formed on 15th of April, 1992. The Defence addresses this issue on its final brief in paragraphs 11, 22, 123, 212; page 95, under section 7; page 1-5, under section 1; and page 164, under section 1 and 3. The Defence maintains that the creation of the Crisis Staff occurred on 19 April 1992. In response to the outbreak of hostilities and the resulting urgent needs of the civilian population, such as water, electricity, food, et cetera. The Prosecution relies solely on the preamble of this gazette, P124, and cites no corroborating testimony by those actually involved in its creation. The gazette preamble cites no sources for its information, quotes no individuals involved in this issue and does not include an official decision as was customary for articles of that type. The Trial Chamber witness Mitar Mitrovic, secretary of the Assembly, on which testimony the Prosecutor relies, simply is not reliable because he was a secretary of the Assembly, obviously being a jurist, a lawyer, he was in charge for preparation of every documents, as we heard from the testimony of many of Defence witnesses. So this particular story that Mr. Mitrovic stated here before this Trial Chamber that Dr. Simic made some kind of editorial attempts is absolutely unsustainable. In fact, there is no official document establishing the Crisis Staff or listing its membership. This is due to the fact that in the days after the outbreak of hostilities on 17th of April, 1992, a number of Municipal Assemblymen and civilian officials made spontaneous attempts to organise a body to coordinate efforts to address the living conditions of the civilian population during war. However, several witnesses testified that the Crisis Staff was in fact officially formed on 19 April 1992, with the adoption of the document under the title "Introduction of a State of Emergency in the Territory of Samac Municipality." This is corroborated by the testimony of Mirko Lukic, transcript 12683 and 12874; then Simeon Simic, transcript 13024; and Lazar Mirkic, transcript 18900. In addition, Trial Chamber witness Mitar Mitrovic testified that he was told either on 18 of April or 19 of April that "a temporary Crisis Staff," and I'm quoting, "would need to be organised or rather established as an ad hoc body to function on a temporary basis," transcript 18697. In conclusion, the editorial-like preamble to the gazette cites no sources for its information, quotes no officials involved in Crisis Staff formation. Further, several witnesses, including a Trial Chamber witness, testified that the Crisis Staff was in fact formed in response to the outbreak of hostilities in the region. Moreover, the fact that the Crisis Staff in Samac municipality was formed after attacks by Croat forces pursuant to the creation of Croatian community of Bosnian Posavina refutes the Prosecution's allegations that its formation was a part of some prearranged plan for a takeover of the region. Clearly, in the specific case of Samac, there is no evidence to suggest that the creation of the Crisis Staff had any connection to so-called variant A and B document allegedly issued five months before. And, Your Honour, just take a look on the territory in Bosnian Posavina occupied by Muslim and Croat forces at that time, and you will see that the only island within the region of controlling by Muslim and Croat forces was Samac. Logic calls to conclusion that if there was a plan to occupy a region by Serb forces, then how it's possible that it was not done? And furthermore, due to the fact of military political objectives of Muslim and Croat side at the beginning of July 1992, the military operation called corridor was launched by VRS. Why this operation should be launched, if the Serbian forces controlled all this territory in accordance with the previous plans, as alleged by the Prosecution. It's not logical. In paragraph 117, the Prosecution states that Dr. Simic was present at the meeting in Obudovac on 15th of April, 1992, where he said: "Crisis Staff was to meet the next night to ensure that civilian authorities would be ready to swing into action to make sure the government still worked." The Prosecution cites only the testimony of its star witness, Stevan Todorovic, whose testimony the Trial Chamber itself has warned should be taken with caution, with regard to this particular allegation. Furthermore, Todorovic himself conceded that Dr. Simic was in fact not present at that meeting, transcript 9905. In paragraph 118, the Prosecution alleges that Dr. Simic's presence in Crkvina from where the Lugar group commenced its attack on 17 April 1992 indicates his participation in a joint criminal enterprise. Again, the Prosecution relies heavily on the testimony of Stevan Todorovic, whose credibility is suspect. In this instance, Todorovic stated that, among others, Trial Chamber witness Mitar Mitrovic was present in Crkvina, which Mr. Mitrovic denies, transcript 18809-10. Of the others who Todorovic said were present at the meeting, Bozo Ninkovic testified that he spent the night between 16th and 17th of April at his sister's house, transcript 13507-8. Further, next person mentioned by Todorovic allegedly present in Crkvina, Simeon Simic testified that he spent that night at his family house in Kruskovo Polje, and in response to Her Honour Judge Mumba's questioning, admitted that he only learned about what happened that night on 19 April at the first meeting of the Crisis Staff, transcript 13003-4. At any rate, Dr. Simic acknowledges being in Crkvina on 17th of April, 1992. After he and other doctors were called early in the morning of 17th of April by an army duty officer and told to go to Crkvina to tend to the wounded. At the time of the call, Dr. Simic was at his family home in. Dr. Simic was the only doctor to respond to this call and tended to several wounded soldiers. Indeed Dr. Simic's testimony is confirmed by the fact that, as the Prosecution itself cites, Zaric's brother-in-law, Fadil Topcagic, he saw Dr. Simic tending to a wounded soldier. See Prosecution brief paragraph 118. The fact that Dr. Simic, a physician, was summoned from his home to tend the wounded soldiers on the night hostilities broke out can hardly be said to show beyond a reasonable doubt that he intended to participate in joint criminal enterprise. In paragraph 128, the Prosecution alleges that Dr. Simic called Colonel Nikolic at 3.00 a.m. on 17th of April to inform him that Serb forces were taking over Bosanski Samac. Dr. Simic denied he made this call. In addition, several witnesses, including the Prosecution's own witnesses, testified that the telephone lines were cut during the time this call was alleged to have taken place. Prosecution witness Dragan Lukac, transcript 1653-4, testified that the phone lines were cut when he tried to make a call around 2.25 a.m. on 17 of April, 1992, and were still cut when he tried to make a call from a neighbour's house shortly thereafter. Chief of police, Dragan Lukac, testified to that. Prosecution witness Sulejman Tihic, head of state of Bosnia now and prominent lawyer, testified, transcript 1358-9. So he similarly testified that the phone lines were down for about three hours in the early morning hours of 17th of April. He further testified that the phone lines were still down at 3.00 a.m., the very time the Prosecution now says Dr. Simic made this call. Commander of Muslim military unit, Prosecution witness Alija Fitozovic, testified on transcript 8509 that the phone lines were not operational again until around 5.00 a.m., and moreover, Todorovic, the crown witness, the top witness of the Prosecution, testified, transcript 9086, that the 4th Detachment was tasked with the responsibility of disconnecting the phone lines at 3.00 a.m. And so, I'm quoting: "Not one single phone in the municipality was functioning." Thus it is clear from the Prosecution's own witnesses that Dr. Simic could not have made this call. In addition to that, I'm just quoting several examples, but we have many Prosecution witnesses testifying that at that time, the critical time, the phones were cut off in Bosanski Samac. Indeed, Colonel Nikolic appears to be the only witness present in Bosanski Samac that night who believes the phone lines were working, and furthermore, the Prosecution relies, they are desperate to make this evidence, to prove their theory, so the Prosecution relies only on testimony of Colonel Nikolic. You can see in its brief, for its assertation here, despite the testimony of several other of their own witnesses that such call could not have been made. And it is not disputed that the Lugar group was under the command of Colonel Nikolic, and given this fact, it is beyond the bounds of reason to suggest that Dr. Simic, as a civilian functionary, did not control authority over any police or military forces, would call Colonel Nikolic to state that the Crisis Staff had taken over Bosanski Samac while the 7.000 soldiers of the 17th Tactical Group also under the command of Colonel Nikolic were supposedly asleep in their barracks. The Defence asserts the testimony of Colonel Nikolic, Zaric, and Simeunovic, as well as the other witnesses from the military should be treated with caution due to the fact that these men have tried to shift the blame from the military authorities responsible for the acts occurring throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina municipality to Dr. Simic. And Prosecution tried to create a notion that Dr. Simic should be a scapegoat along -- along civil -- so Dr. Simic along civilian functionary with no power or authority to control or to stop them, Lugar group and the other perpetrators within the police and military chain of command. Lastly, the Prosecution again contradicts itself. In paragraph 121, the Prosecution states that the Trial Chamber should accept that communication occurred between Dr. Simic and Colonel Nikolic. That's a conclusion. However, in a footnote to this same sentence, footnote 186, the Prosecution concedes that the phone lines were disconnected for several crucial hours in the early morning of 17th of April, 1992, as the Serb forces seized control. In paragraph 127, the Prosecution, without citing any evidence, states that SDS dominated Crisis Staff seized the organs if civilian government -- of civilian government with the assistance of the military. The Prosecution, without citing any evidence, recklessly and repeatedly uses term such as SDS-dominated Crisis Staff, or Dr. Simic's Crisis Staff. However, the Prosecution has presented no evidence that the Crisis Staff was dominated by the SDS or that Dr. Simic wielded any particular authority. Indeed, the Prosecution statement appeared to reflect a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of the municipal civilian government in Bosanski Samac. By contrast, the Defence has provided substantial evidence that several members of the Crisis Staff in fact did not belong to SDS. Savo Popovic was a member of SDP, socialist party of B and H, headed by a Muslim. Simeon Simic was a member of the Liberal Party, again headed by a Muslim. Miroslav Tadic belonged to no party. He was independent. As for the term "seized," the Prosecution failed to present evidence that the Crisis Staff seized the municipal organs of government. The Defence has shown that the Bosnia-Herzegovina was in the process of dissolution from October 1991 until the Dayton Peace Accords in 1995. In Bosanski Samac, all three ethnic communities in B and H established their own political and legal systems. In Bosanski Samac, all three ethnic groups established their own Crisis Staffs. For example, the Serb faction established their Crisis Staff in one part of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, and the Croats and Muslims established an analogous Crisis Staff in another part of the municipality called Bosanski Samac Domaljevac, Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac Domaljevac. Thus the evidence shows in no way can the SDS or Crisis Staff be said to have seized control over the municipal organs, because, as I said, three constituent nations in Bosnia throughout the period of 1991 until 1995 formed their own organs and institutions. At any rate, the context under which the Prosecution alleges this seizure includes no specific reference to Dr. Simic personally. In fact, the Prosecution's version of events centres entirely on the role of the police and military, two organs over which Dr. Simic and the Crisis Staff had no de facto or de jure control. In paragraphs 124 until 132, there is no mention of Dr. Simic or Crisis Staff except in part of paragraph 138, and in 138 the Prosecution cites as evidence of the Crisis Staff's role in the alleged takeover and alleged meeting in Belgrade in May or June 1992 between the Crisis Staff, Zaric, senior members of SFRY military regarding the appointment of Crni as commander of 2nd Posavina Brigade. With regard to the above-mentioned Prosecution submission, the Defence introduced overwhelming evidence that Dr. Simic was not either mastermind or participant in the military and police operations within the municipality of Bosanski Samac. And with regard to the Prosecution's submission relating to the report of General Wilmot, I already addressed that issue earlier this morning. In paragraph 140, the Prosecution cites the Crisis Staff order to a -- to a disarmament issue, it's Exhibit P77, to suggest it related to some illegal takeover of power. The Defence addressed this issue in its brief in page 149 under 2 and pages 150 and 151. In the first place, there is nothing to suggest this order was discriminatory nature. The order was an attempt to ensure the safety of all citizens by removing illegal weapons from the community. Indeed, the order applies to all citizens regardless of ethnicity and the Prosecution has offered no evidence to suggest otherwise. Rather, all citizens were allowed to possess only those weapons which were authorised by the military and/or police. Further, several witnesses testified that the --

utterances.text: I do apologise. This was confirmed by the testimony of Zaric, transcript 20051-54. Then Radovan Antic, transcript 16746-52. Jovo Savic, transcript 17029-31. And Stevan Nikolic, transcript 18559-61. Given the fact of war and the operation of so-called paramilitaries in the area, this order constitutes a legitimate effort to provide for the safety of the local civilian population. And what we said in our brief, since there is handwriting details on that brief and there is no signature on that document, in details we explained that it cannot be ascribed neither to Crisis Staff nor to Dr. Simic personally. Paragraph 141, the Prosecution asserts that the declaration of state of emergency, Exhibit P89 and ter, yes, in Bosanski Samac was a textbook coup d'etat manoeuvre. The Defence addresses this issue on page 155 of its brief. This order coincided with the establishment of the Crisis Staff and indeed the state of emergency was its raison d'etre. While the Prosecution shows -- chooses to mischaracterise this order as a textbook coup d'etat manoeuvre, it ignores one very important fact: War had broken out in Bosanski Samac. Thus there was in fact a state of emergency. Rather, the Prosecution seems to suggest that the war does not constitute an emergency, an untenable position. In addition, the Prosecution conveniently fails to note that the creation of a Crisis Staff in times of emergency, such as during a flood, earthquake, or war, was a standard procedure in the former Yugoslavia, dating back to at least 1945. Indeed, Crisis Staff has been created on several occasions over the years prior to this war in times of emergency, such as natural disasters, et cetera. Does the Prosecution suggest that the previous creation of this Crisis Staff was likewise a textbook for coup d'etat manoeuvre? Indeed the Serbian community's Crisis Staff was formed only after attacks by Croat and Muslim forces in the municipality and in response to the fact that the Municipal Assembly of Serb people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo had stopped functioning. Furthermore, the Prosecution also conveniently fails to note that in addition to the Serb Crisis Staff, the Croat community also formed a Crisis Staff of its own, as I mentioned earlier, in the other part of municipality of Bosanski Samac. In paragraphs 142 to 149, 151 to 158, and 166 to 176 of its final trial brief, the Prosecution alleges that as an important step in furtherance of their plan to ethnically cleanse the Serb-held territory, Serb municipal and military authorities, including Blagoje Simic's SDS-controlled Crisis Staff, and Dr. Simic himself, systematically arrested, detained, and mistreated Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim civilians based on religious, ethnic, and political affiliations. The Prosecution alleges that the military forced hundreds of men, women, and children from their homes and took them to Zasavica. The central goal of the Crisis Staff being ethnic separation by force. In its attempt to establish a connection between the Bosnian Serb leadership and the civilian authorities of Bosanski Samac in terms of ethnic cleansing and separation, the Prosecution particularly relies on Exhibit P5, Decision on Strategic Objective of Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, adopted by the Republika Srpska People's Assembly on May 12, 1992 and published, I'm underlining that, published in the Republika Srpska Official Gazette number 22 on November 26, 1993. The Defence addresses this document in detail in our page 137 and 138 of our brief. In sum, in addition to bearing no discriminatory insignia, this document, although adopted in May 1992, was publicised only in late 1993 and therefore remained unknown to local civilian authorities. Dr. Simic testified that he had no personal knowledge of this document and that it had never been discussed by the civilian authorities of the Samac municipality. Accordingly, the Defence reiterates that the Prosecution allegations are unsubstantiated and therefore must fail for absence of any nexus between the Samac civilian authorities and this document. Throughout its brief, in paragraphs 43, 199, 217, 234, 235, 238, 258 to 273, 309, 310, 325 to 336, 481, 486, 487, 519, 586, 648, et cetera, the Defence has clearly shown that neither the Crisis Staff in general, nor Dr. Simic in particular, were in any manner whatsoever involved in arrests and/or detention of non-Serbs in Samac, nor were they aware of crimes committed by Stevan Todorovic. The army and the police, over which they had no de jure or de facto command and control. No military or police reports regarding arrests and treatment of detained individuals were ever filed with the Crisis Staff or Dr. Simic, who was by law without authority to control or to affect to continue the detention in different centres in Samac. In addition, several witnesses testified that the detentions and trial proceedings against the non-Serbs were based on a reasonable suspicions that the persons were illegally armed and preparing illegal attacks against the Serb population. Both Prosecution and Defence witnesses gave ample evidence about the police and the army playing decisive roles in arrests and detention, as well as the searches of houses and collection of weapons. By contrast, the Defence again underscores and draws attention to the numerous examples of good acts of conduct of civilian authorities in Samac towards citizens of all three ethnic groups, which is corroborated in a number of witness testimonies. Then in paragraph 145 until 149, Prosecution stated that the local police, members of 4th Detachment and paramilitary forces participated in the collection of weapons immediately after the forcible takeover. As stated in pages 149 and 159, and elsewhere in its brief, the Defence acknowledges the Prosecution assertation that the police and the army were in charge of collecting weapons and searching houses. It is not in dispute. In fact, confiscation of weapons solely within the authority of the army and the police. This is also confirmed by many witnesses, called both by Defence and the Prosecution. Furthermore, the Prosecution thesis of the paramilitary forces also being involved in the collection of weapons corroborates the Defence assertation that the Lugar group was in fact deeply involved with the police and the army and under their command and control. The Prosecution produced no credible or sufficient evidence to link either Dr. Simic or Crisis Staff with these activities. This in particular as the time the collection of weapons was taking place and which is referred to by the Prosecution as immediately after the takeover that the Crisis Staff had not even been established yet. The Prosecution states in its para 146 that the Crisis Staff commemorated that of a notorious paramilitary Aleksandar Vukovic by establishing the Vuk foundation. We addressed this issue in general in our -- page 143 of our brief, just to say that the absolutely unsustainable position of the Prosecution in claiming that the naming the foundation after a volunteer indicates some kind of discriminatory intent. The decision on establishment of this foundation was aimed at setting up of humanitarian fund to provide aid and wounded combatants and families of fallen combatants. And it is very clear for the wordings of this decision. The Prosecution alleges that Dr. -- that Blagoje Simic SDS controlled Crisis Staff ordered that all people of Croatian nationality be arrested and isolated and taken to vital facilities in town, paragraph 166. The Prosecution persistently invokes the Exhibit P71 as an obvious example of the Crisis Staff involvement in the detention of non-Serbs in Samac. The Prosecution errs, as shown by the Defence on page 9091 and elsewhere in its final brief. There is no credible evidence that Dr. Simic even signed this document, not to mention the fact that several stamps, identical to one of these decisions, were in circulation and were used without authorisation or any control over their use. Several Defence witnesses, members of the Crisis Staff, and Dr. Simic included, categorically deny that the Crisis Staff adopted this decision. Both Prosecution and Defence witnesses corroborated on numerous occasions that military and police authorities were in fact in charge of these procedures, which is also stated in the decision itself. The wording of this decision is customary to police and military. Vital objects. We address that issue in the other part of our brief. So it's customary for military and police not for civilian officials, and this clearly indicates that the document originates from those circles. The Prosecution contradicts itself by relying on this document at the same time as it admits that in Samac there was no reported cases of the placement of Croats in vital facilities. Even the Prosecution witness Todorovic stated that the Crisis Staff had never discussed the isolation of the non-Serb inhabitants of Samac. Again, the overwhelming evidence and testimony produced and presented during trial that this very Crisis Staff was composed of individuals coming from different or even on political parties then in existence. There is no sufficient or reliable evidence in this case to prove otherwise, so this is unfounded and misleading Prosecution assertation must fall with regard to Dr. Simic's Crisis Staff or SDS Crisis Staff. Your Honour, is it time for our half an hour break?
