utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Another part of the Prosecution's submission is related actually it was stated in paragraphs 170 to 174, that the Serb civilian and military rulers of Bosanski Samac operated three general types of detention facilities for their widespread and systematic persecution of the non-Serbs, specifying police station, TO building, primary and secondary school complex, Crkvina and the village of Zasavica. Throughout the trial proceedings and its final brief the Defence produced sufficient evidence to clearly show that: Number one: The police station, TO building, primary and secondary school were never under the competency and control of either the Crisis Staff or Dr. Simic. Number 2: Co-defendant Tadic gave evidence that the Crisis Staff never either discussed the issue of formation of detention centres or was asked permission for their establishment. Transcript 15274. Number 3: Police and military were directly in charge and responsible for these facilities. Number 4: Neither Todorovic, nor any member of the military were even members of the Crisis Staff or War Presidency. Number 5: Dr. Simic was never in a position to oversee or control the acts of the police or army and there was no obligation to their part to report to the Crisis Staff and Dr. Simic. Number 6: The Prosecution witness Todorovic testified on 7 June 2002, I'm quoting, the highest responsibility for the protection of the detainees lay with me." Number 7: Todorovic also testified that he had orally informed the Crisis Staff on, inter alia, the prison and the people that were detained, but only generally and not about all the details, as stated by the Prosecution. This evidence, however, does not prove that Dr. Simic was informed about it since Todorovic refers to Crisis Staff, it being a collective body and not to Dr. Simic personally. Not to mention that Todorovic speaks about informing them orally and in general, from which one cannot infer that the Crisis Staff could have full, if any, concrete knowledge of the actual situation in prisons. Number 7: Blatant inconsistencies in the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses Hasan Bicic, Muhamed Bicic, Ibrahim Salkic and Dragan Delic regarding Dr. Simic's coming or presence to primary and secondary school together with Todorovic raised profound doubts in the credibility of these witnesses and veracity of their accounts of events. This testimony, it is submitted, should not be afforded any weight, particularly due to the fact that not only Dr. Simic himself but also Prosecution witness Todorovic denies Dr. Simic was ever present in any of the facilities mentioned, as well as Simo Zaric's driver Teodor Tutnjevic, transcript 17467. Number 8: The village of Crkvina was within the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group, over which Dr. Simic had no power whatsoever. Number 9: Transport of civilians to and from Crkvina was organised and carried out by the military. The Prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that if at all any nexus between Dr. Simic and arrest and detention taking place in Bosanski Samac. By ignoring the evidence and unfoundedly placing impossible amount of power in Dr. Simic's hands, the Prosecution is simply trying to twist and mischaracterise a clear and obvious fact, that all powers over detention facilities in Bosanski Samac were within police and the military. With regard to the village of Zasavica referred to by the Prosecution as an isolation site, the Defence respectfully reminds that ample evidence was produced during trial about the composition of population, living conditions in Zasavica, and activities of the civilian municipal authorities aimed at securing sufficient foodstuffs and other things for this village. The Defence has provided detailed submission on this issue in its final brief, particularly paragraphs 24, 272, 273, 303, 309, 544, 567, 586, as well on the pages 145 and 184. In sum, civilian municipal authorities provided livestock feed, chicken feed, and cattle feed for Croat farmers in Zasavica. Civilian authorities provided facilities for the education of all children in Zasavica. Medical care for all people irrespective of their ethnicity was arranged by setting up an infirmary. Many Defence witnesses conditions in terms of housing, food, accommodation and hygiene were quite satisfactory, in some instances even better than in Samac. Large number of Serb refugees coming from all parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina were also accommodated in Zasavica. The Defence submits that given the facts described above, corroborated by many witnesses and evidence, one cannot speak about any kind of isolation of the non-Serb population. Even if accepting the Prosecution thesis, a question inevitably arises: Were the Serb inhabitants of Zasavica also isolated? It is simply impossible to isolate one part of the ethnically mixed village and not to isolate the rest of it and therefore the Prosecution assertation must fall. In paragraph 185, the Prosecution alleges that Dr. Simic and Todorovic brought paramilitaries to the municipality to assist in a takeover. The Defence addresses this issue in greater details in paragraph 215, 216, 474, 475, 603, as well as the page 141 [phoen] and page 169 under the 10 and was also in its Exhibit D177/1. Here the Prosecution makes -- must make a giant leap of logic in an effort to implicate Dr. Simic in military and police activities. At the outset, the Defence again stresses that Dr. Simic and the Crisis Staff did not exercise any control over the police and military units. They simply did not have the power to control the acts of those conducting the hostilities. In addition, the evidence overwhelmingly shows that the arrival of the group was a military operation. The evidence shows that Lugar group arrived in territory of Samac in military helicopters, Exhibit P17. They were under the command of 17th Tactical Group, P127 and transcript 18997. They participated in military actions under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, Exhibits P174, P175, and transcript 18997. Nikolic and Lugar were from the same town in Serbia. In addition, several witnesses testified that neither Dr. Simic nor the municipal chapter of SDS had any connection to the arrival of the Lugar group. Further, Prosecution witness Todorovic admitted that Dr. Simic had no contacts with Bogdanovic or Jovanovic concerning the Lugar groups coming to Samac from Serbia. Finally, the Prosecution's own footnote to paragraph 185, footnote 400, concedes that the Lugar group was under the authority of the police, an organ almost completely independent from the civilian Crisis Staff. In addition to the other evidences provided by the Prosecution with regard to the command authority of Colonel Nikolic. With regard to paragraph 187, the Defence would like to reiterate its -- these are the events regarding the killing of Anto Brandic, Mr. Anto Brandic, and a Croat nicknamed Dikan. The Defence reiterates its position that it's not -- it's a part of the Todorovic plea bargain agreement and just in terms of precision, we would like to address this matter. First and foremost, the Defence could not but note in this paragraph 187 the Prosecution actually speaks of two killings, which occurred on two different dates, 26th of April, 1992, and 29 of July, 1992. And these killings were allegedly committed by two different perpetrators, first Lugar and the second Todorovic and other police officers. In this particular paragraph, while the name of the victims is the same, Anto Brandic, only the two different nicknames, Dikan and Antesa, therefore unclear to the Defence whether the Prosecution errs in the victim's name or in dates alleged, especially since none of the witness testimony presented during trial identifies with precision the person or persons in question. So my submission is rather in terms of the detail of the -- I'm not going to enter into this particular axiom, of course. Ascribing these cases to the Crisis Staff, it's impossible. The Defence addressed this issue in paragraphs 483 and 485. And now the Defence further states that the Prosecution again appears to fundamentally misunderstand the nature of the power structure in Bosanski Samac, repeatedly suggesting incorrectly that local civilian authorities had authority over police and military units. Even assuming, arguendo [phoen], that Dr. Simic and the Crisis Staff were informed of this murder, they were by law powerless to do anything about it. The military and the police were obliged to take necessary actions against the perpetrators of the crime. This clearly was an unlawful act by the members of the police and military. In no way can the acts of Todorovic or other soldiers and police who were under the command and authority of 17th Tactical Group and the regional public security station in Doboj be attributed to the local civilian authorities and Dr. Simic himself. Stated simply, the soldiers who perpetrated this murder were not acting on behalf of the Crisis Staff. They were acting in their capacity as soldiers or individually as loose cannons. Indeed, Prosecution witness Todorovic, who confessed to being an accomplice to the murder of Dikan himself conceded that by the law -- by law of the military was the organ with the appropriate jurisdiction to investigate the murder and that neither the Crisis Staff, nor Dr. Simic had authority to even conduct an investigation. Transcript 9923-24. Moreover, Todorovic testified that he only informally notified members of the Crisis Staff about what was happening. Further indicating that no formal report to or action by the Crisis Staff was customary or required. Indeed, a formal report about the incident was required to be filed not with the Crisis Staff, but rather to the regional centre of public security in Doboj, as is consistent with the chain of command of police, transcript 9930-31. Todorovic also stated that Dr. Simic and the other members of the Crisis Staff were shocked when they learned of the murders and called for the appropriate military and judicial authorities to take action, the only course of action open to civilian authorities.

utterances.text: Thank you. And these few minutes, of course, which brings me to ... In paragraph 187, the Prosecution again attempts to mischaracterise the relationship between the police and civilian authorities. The Prosecution also seeks to hold Dr. Simic liable for the shooting deaths of Barto Kljajic and Marko Evic at the hands of the Lugar group, solely on the basis that Todorovic testified that he informed the Crisis Staff of the murders after the fact. Dr. Simic was unaware of these killings. Even Todorovic himself in his testimony never specifically stated that he had informed Dr. Simic personally, but only the Crisis Staff in general, which is a collective body encompassed of several persons. In fact, his exact words were: "I think the Crisis Staff knew of this, that it was informed of this verbally," which indicates that Todorovic could not even confirm with certainty that even the Crisis Staff was made aware of these killings. The Prosecution also refers to the testimony of Witness Mladen Borbeli, who also speaking of Lugar killing two people failed to mention their names so one cannot be certain if this witness was actually referring to the same individuals as Todorovic. In conclusion, the Defence witness Ljubomir Vukovic whose testimony the Prosecution also involves in relation to this incident clearly stated that all the people who were actually killed in prison in Samac in SUP, in the school, "as regards all those, we were neither informed nor did we organise their funerals. They were not taken to the morgue, and we in the civil and defence staff, civilian protection defence staff therefore did not know about those people who were killed in prison." That was not accessible to the public. Such knowledge was not accessible to the public. This testimony is another fact in support of the Defence assertion that crimes commit by Todorovic, Lugar group and others were not known to the civilian authorities and population. As stated above, Todorovic himself testified that the Crisis Staff had no authority to conduct an investigation or judicial proceedings against those responsible. These murders were conducted by the Lugar group, a unit under the command and jurisdiction of 17th Tactical Group, by law, it was the responsibility of the military, not the civilian authorities, to take appropriate action to bring those responsible for these murders to justice. In paragraph 188, Prosecution seeks to tie the Crisis Staff to the murders conducted by the Lugar group in Crkvina around 7 May 1992. The Defence addresses these accusations in paragraph 51, 61 to 64, 203 and 484. This is one of the most egregious examples of the Prosecution making unfounded conclusions in the absence of any supporting evidence. The Prosecution states merely that Lugar group committed these acts while working with the Crisis Staff. However, the Prosecution offers no detail -- no details regarding the alleged cooperation and cites no sources for its allegation. With regard to these events in Crkvina, the Defence reiterates again that Zaric, Dr. Simic, and others testified that the massacre of Crkvina has occurred around 8th of May and that neither the Crisis Staff nor Dr. Simic has possessed any authority instigate -- to instigate criminal proceedings against members of military units. In its paragraph 210, Prosecution states that the Crisis Staff was in charge to transfer large number of illegally detained civilians to military custody. The Prosecution did not offer any evidence to that extent. However, the Defence reiterates its previous submission that neither Crisis Staff nor Dr. Simic could carry out these activities. The Defence relies on testimony of Dr. Simic, transcript 12580 -- 82, sorry. And the key Prosecution witness Stevan Todorovic, transcript 9610 and transcript 10118-9. Transfer of detained civilians was solely in the hands of military and police. In relation to paragraphs 212 and 214 of the Prosecution brief, the Defence states the following: Number 1: Dr. Simic was unable to perform his duty within War Presidency throughout at least August of 1992 and after, and the following months, since he was wounded and he received medical treatment. Number 2: All events regarding Zasavica were out of Dr. Simic's powers and competencies. Number 3: Even the Prosecution admits in its paragraph 254 that in August 1992, around 200 non-Serbs of military age were called to a meeting at Spomen Dom, in order to be relieved of work obligation if they took up arms of Republika Srpska. This meeting was organised by the military, and since great majority of non-Serbs refused to respond to that offer, all of them swum across the Sava River that night. Number 4: In response to that action, Stevan Todorovic issued an order banning gathering of three or more non-Serbs in town, and soon after, military and police transferred a number of family members of non-Serbs who escaped from Samac to village of Zasavica. The Defence reiterates again its position regarding the concept of work obligation and the organs who were in charge of it. We address that issue in our paragraphs 341 and 342. Compelling evidence presented during trial clearly shows that Dr. Simic was never present at the house with the swimming pool in Odzak. In fact, in August 1992, Dr. Simic was wounded and medically treated, so he was unable to be in two places at the same time. Dr. Simic's testimony supported and corroborated by another Defence witness, Savo Popovic, a member of the civilian council of military administration in Odzak. Savo Popovic testified that due to the lack of electricity and the swimming pool was empty of water, that Dr. Simic in addition had never been present near the pool or house in Odzak and that in any case, the Samac municipal authorities had no influence on the work obligation that was carried out in Odzak because it was in the hands of military administration. The evidence presented by the Defence deeply undermines testimonies of the said two Prosecution witnesses to whom therefore no particular weight should be afforded. And in addition, the Prosecution relies on the words of Witness K, saying that Mr. Kapetanovic told her that her name had been selected by the Crisis Staff computer. This is impossible in this time of war and we have many testimonies that the Crisis Staff was not in possession of commuter. On page 4626, Witness K testified with regard to the computer. The summons I received had an illegible signature but when I spoke to Mr. Kapetanovic he said that my name had been selected by the Crisis Staff computer. And then she went to say: "As far as I know, it was Mr. Milan Simic who was in charge of the work assignments." So there is not any relation -- there is not any word in the testimony of Witness K relating to Dr. Simic. And also Defence witness Simeon Simic stated on 13048-9 that there was no computer in Crisis Staff. With regard to the issuance of orders and policies and decisions by Dr. Simic on the discriminatory basis, we addressed this particular issue in numerous paragraphs in our brief, because this is core of defence case. We are showing that, number 1, the decisions were not discriminatory in the nature; number 2, the overwhelming defence evidence with regard to the humanitarian activities and aid and work of Dr. Simic and the other members of municipal authorities clearly shows that there is not any basis to claim that Dr. Simic was a participant in some kind of discriminatory process in Samac. With regard to the paragraph 274 of Prosecution brief, we can say that 17th of April indeed was designed as a Samac municipal holiday. But there is no particular decision on that. It was adopted by the Municipal Assembly on May 12, 1993, by majority of the Assemblymen votes and applied only to part of Serbian municipality, whereas the Croatian part has their own holidays. Number 2: The Prosecution failed to produce any evidence to the extent that Dr. Simic voted in favour or against these particular [indiscernible], whether he was present at that session, and it is absolutely unclear for the Defence what is the basis of the submission of the Prosecution with regard to Dr. Simic with this particular issue. And Madam President, Your Honours, this brings me to my third and final chapter, final part of my argument, but before that, I also would like to say that the Defence in the list that it was provided to Your Honours with regard to the wanton and extensive plundering and looting of non-Serb property as stated by the Prosecution address this issue in numerous paragraphs, at least 30 paragraphs of our brief. So we clearly explain that there was not any relation with Dr. Simic. I will discuss the Prosecution key witness Mr. Todorovic, a man who, by the Prosecution's own admission, has to be viewed with caution and who Judge Hunt, and this is transcript 805-8, and then transcript 813-4, foresaw the problems the Prosecution was creating by making a deal with such an unsavory character, whereby in essence the Prosecution gave him a licence to lie. Who is Mr. Todorovic? A self-proclaimed member of the Crisis Staff, a wannabe, but not just any kind of wannabe. For the usual wannabe's are those who have no power, who seek attention, who seek affection, who seek to be important. No. Mr. Todorovic is a man of power that comes not by virtue of the law but rather by the virtue of the gun. By virtue of his connections in the underworld, the fringe elements, a man who was able to use his authority and his position and the power that came with it to commit acts of unspeakable evil. And as I have indicated earlier, he was nothing than a warlord with his own little private army, coming and going as it pleased, coming to meetings, invited or not, displaying an aura of self-importance to act outside the law. Who among us here would buy a used car from Mr. Todorovic based on his representations of the quality of the car? On direct examination, he says one thing and on a cross-examination he contradicts himself. He makes claims that cannot be substantiated and as I have indicated in order to get himself out of the situation that he found himself in, he lied to Prosecution, to the Prosecution, told them what he thought they wanted to hear. And of course his deal with the Prosecution is contingent and allows him repeating his lies. And so even if by some miracle his conscience was evacuant to the point where he would want to speak the truth, to accept his full responsibility, to explain his independent actions, if that were to occur, he would not be able to do so because he would lose his deal with the Prosecution. One could speak for hours about Mr. Todorovic, but there are two points I would like to leave with this Trial Chamber. Point number 1: And the Prosecution in so much admitted in their opening statement that he's not credible, he's not reliable, he is not trustworthy, he is not honest, and that anything he says must be viewed with caution. Words of the Prosecution, transcript 940-42. And point number 2: There was one instance in the trial when the Prosecution did pose a question to him. I'm quoting the question of the Prosecution. It's paragraph -- it's a transcript 9119. Question of the Prosecution: "And you mentioned earlier in an answer that you just gave that you occasionally had problems with the Crisis Staff and with the army over releasing people. What sort of problem did you experience?" Todorovic's answer was: "As far as I remember, I had problems with members of the army, not the Crisis Staff, but on two or three occasions with the army. And if need be, I can also explain these two or three cases." And what was the Prosecution's response when Mr. Todorovic said: I can explain? The Prosecution at that point thought that Mr. Todorovic just might have explained how the Crisis Staff and Dr. Simic had nothing to do with what was going on and that it was the military that was causing problems. But the Prosecution, ever so willing to assist the Trial Chamber in knowing the truth, said, and I quote: "No, that won't be necessary. That won't be necessary, Mr. Todorovic." This little example speaks for itself. The Prosecution simply is disinterested in allowing you to have all of the facts. Because if that were the case, then you might conclude, as I suggest you should, that Dr. Simic in his individual capacity as a speaker of the Crisis Staff or as a member of the Crisis Staff was not in control, he had no authority, he had no effective power, did not participate in any unlawful activities, and had no resources available to contain either Mr. Todorovic, his associates, or anyone else that was engaged in any criminal activity. Although, as I underscored earlier in my brief, Dr. Simic did on several occasions notify the appropriate authorities of the crimes being committed by certain perpetrators in Bosanski Samac. The third thing is, and I respectfully ask this Trial Chamber to keep that in mind: That it is a fact that it has been well established that Dr. Simic was not fond of Mr. Todorovic, that Mr. Todorovic certainly was not fond of Dr. Simic, who, after all, opposed Mr. Todorovic's nomination to his position of the chief of police, which occurred prior to the formation of the Crisis Staff. And even prior to the events in Bosanski Samac leading up to the indictment and events where Todorovic found responsible. And then there is a question: Would someone like Mr. Todorovic, whom we know and be cautioned by the Prosecution to view with caution, would he have given his prior history with Dr. Simic, having incentive to implicate, to embellish, and to lie about Dr. Simic, especially if there is something to be gained, such as a deal from the Prosecution? Madam President and Your Honours, with your indulgence, I would like to sum up my oral submissions, and in doing so, I think it would be only fitting to raise or to pose certain questions which we have yet to hear from Prosecution, for, after all, they have the burden of proof. They have to prove each and every element beyond a reasonable doubt, for each count in the indictment. So I ask, number 1: When the Prosecution gets up to do its rebuttal, perhaps they can explain how is it that non-Serbs who were on their way to leaving Bosanski Samac decided to stay and when they stay, nothing ever happened to them? Number 2: How is it that Serb choose to leave Bosanski Samac? Number 3: Was there a campaign to expel them, to persecute them, to cleanse up area from them? Is that what it is? Perhaps they can give us an explanation of that. Number 4: How is it that non-Serbs continued to be employed in various sectors in Bosanski Samac if the intent was to ethnically cleanse and persecute? Why would they be kept in position where they could utilise their skills and their talents and their knowledge? For instance, the appointment of the Crisis Staff by Crisis Staff of Dr. Mesud Nogic, a Muslim, respected doctor as a coordinator for the medical centre in Samac? We have the evidence to that extent. Engagement of the non-Serb firefighters, employment in municipal pharmacy, employment of great number of non-Serbs in various public institutions and companies. Number 5: How is it that the Prosecution maintains that Dr. Simic could order or control or prevent Mr. Todorovic in his capacity as the chief of police while at the same time the Prosecution itself deliberately choose to dismiss any counts under Article 7(3) against Dr. Simic? Number 6: How is it Dr. Simic was in pursuit of policy of persecution that he provided medical service and in particular chemodialysis on the non-discriminatory basis to whoever needed it? Perhaps the Prosecution can explain this also. Perhaps the Prosecution can explain how it's possible to persecute someone who has lived in his own house before, during the war, and after the war, in particular, I'm referring to the -- to 10.000 non-Serbs in the Domaljevac area. Number 8: Perhaps the Prosecution can explain how is it that they hold Dr. Simic responsible for military activities, including the exchange of prisoners, when those functions were exclusively under the command and control of the military and republican level? And of course as I noted earlier, if that had been the case, how is it there are no charges under 7(3)? Number 9: Perhaps the Prosecution can explain how is it that Dr. Simic was engaged in persecution by issuing hundreds of orders for betterment of the entire community, irrespective of their ethnic background or religious belief? Is that a form of persecution? I raise all these questions, Your Honours, because I dare say the Prosecutors did not answer them throughout the proceedings. Certainly provided no explanation in its written submission and it has omitted to offer any credible argument in its oral submission. In short, the Prosecution has failed to meet its burden of proof, and these questions that I have just raised demonstrate the Prosecution's failure to establish that Dr. Simic was engaged in any criminal activity that would justify the charges in the indictment. Your Honours, on behalf of Dr. Simic, I would like to thank you for your attention. I would also like to thank you if any members of the Chamber has any question you would like me to address. I'm here to answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. We don't have any questions at this stage. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An officially, good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence of Miroslav Tadic wishes to make its final arguments in the following way: We do not wish to repeat things from our final brief. We primarily wish to speak in view of the facts and whatever else we read in the Prosecutor's brief, as well as what we heard from the Prosecutor. Our concept of our closing argument will be as follows: First I shall address the Trial Chamber with regard to general legal allegations and issues, and then my colleague Mr. Krgovic will speak about the actual charges of persecution that have to do with the forcible takeover of power, illegal arrests, and inhumane treatment, since he worked most actively on those parts of our final brief too. After that, I shall speak about forced labour, deportation, forcible expulsions, et cetera, within the charges of persecution, and then I shall also be referring to the second and third counts in the indictment. Finally, I will have a few words to say in view of the sentencing recommendation made by the Prosecution. At the very outset, I have to present clearly our position with regard to the -- to our assessment of the final brief made by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor does not have a case against Miroslav Tadic. In fact, the Prosecution did not have a case against Miroslav Tadic at the beginning of this trial, and by the end of the trial, the case was completely lost. The evidence that supported the Prosecution case, at the end of the Prosecution case, in terms of the standard that is required on the basis of Rule 98 bis, after the Defence case, when the trial was coming to an end, they even lost the weight that mere indicia have. This compelled the Prosecution to try to introduce new evidence even during the case. Forgetting or disregarding the principle of reciprocal discovery, the Prosecutors kept trying to bring in new evidence that was disclosed a day or two before it was actually exhibited, although the Prosecution had had these documents for years. They tried to introduce evidence yet again that the Trial Chamber had already ruled on and rejected. They were disarmed by their very own witnesses, who had not spoken the truth, and this was proven during the Defence case for Miroslav Tadic. They were not telling the truth in relation to my client. As for the charges brought against Miroslav Tadic, now that the trial has come to an end, the Prosecution had one last resort, and that is a method called construction. They did so by taking sentences out of context. In this procedure, the method was quite simple: To use big words, to level serious accusations, to impose their own way of thinking upon the Court by way of increasing discreditation. Because after all, this brief is not written and closing arguments are not made in the Prosecutor's view only for this Court but also for the general public, for a public which, in the opinion of the Prosecution, wants to hear big words in order to assist attaining the objective of the Tribunal, and that is, reconciliation of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. However, gentlemen of the Prosecution, the Tribunal does not have to achieve this objective only through harsh sentences; it can also be done through fair trials and through acquitting innocent individuals. And I'm confident that that is what will restore confidence within the former Yugoslavia. What this Defence finds encouraging is the fact that after all everything that was written and everything that was said and presented during this trial was done before Judges. The fact that this Honourable Trial Chamber has comprehensive testimonies rather than extracts, they have complete documents, and, as I am profoundly convinced after having spent almost two years in this courtroom, they will look at all of this evidence fully and from all sides. I'm sure that these Honourable Judges did not miss a single detail. They know that any judgement which is based on construction, guesswork, speculation, histrionics is untenable. At the very outset of their brief, the Prosecution said what this trial was all about. However, the Prosecution omitted to say that this was a trial that had to do with a war. This was a trial about life in a town in abnormal conditions and all the consequences that are created by these conditions. We are going to say a few words about that too. This was a trial that had to do about the absurdity of everything that war does to ordinary citizens. Yes. This was a trial about evil, about fear, about suffering, and about pain, but it was also a trial about aid, solidarity, faith, and sacrifice, and about humaneness too, a word that the Prosecution has so scorned when they heard it from the lips of Miroslav Tadic's witnesses. This is also something we're going to refer to in our closing arguments. In this trial, there was a lot of counting, additions, subtraction, et cetera. We were all deeply moved by this, all of us here in the courtroom, when numbers were referred to of persons killed, persons who left, persons who moved in, persons who were exchanged, persons who came back. We knew that after all we were talking about human beings, about their individual fates, and everybody had a moving story to tell. However, it is the Prosecution's numbers that gave rise to this indictment, and they constitute its most important part and the Defence has to speak about this. The position of the Prosecutor is clear. I think that the position of Miroslav Tadic is clear too. It has not changed from its very first statement, and it has not changed from when we first started challenging what the Prosecution witness said and when the Prosecution gave their open statement. I shall describe this in a few words. Miroslav Tadic did not participate at all in political life in the municipality, either before the war or during the war or after the war. Today we heard the Prosecutor say that he was highly ideologically motivated. I really don't know how the Prosecutor has inferred that. What he knew about politics was what an ordinary citizen knows. The Prosecutor did not even deal with his political positions before the war. Before the war, he was a person who was well known among the citizens of Samac and he enjoyed a degree of prominence. His appointment to the position of assistant commander for logistics in the 4th Detachment and in the Crisis Staff are a result of that prominence that he enjoyed and the fact that he was not compromised in any quarters. His work in the civilian defence staff was anything but what the Prosecutor has tried to misconstrue. Tadic did not take part in any activities related to the takeover of vital facilities in town on the 16th and 17th of April. The Prosecution has no evidence to that effect. His work on exchanges is due to his origins and the fact that he knew people on both sides, also that he had a strong wish to help everyone. Miroslav Tadic claims that everything that was done concerning exchanges by the Samac commission was all with a view to helping all people who wanted to have their wishes carried out, either in terms of coming back or going away. I just wish to add a correction. The transcript does not reflect that I did not -- that I said that there is no proof of anything that Miroslav Tadic did in 1991. There is no evidence related to 1991. The Defence claims that the work of that commission was in accordance with the principles that were observed by international organisations, primarily the ICRC, with regard to exchanges. Irrespective of whether it was the only possible solution or a constant principle. Except for less than three months, Tadic did not participate in any way in any important government authorities in the municipality. He was not a member of the War Presidency, he was not appointed president of the commission for exchanges, but he was its member. At the beginning of 1993, he was relieved of his duty as commander of the civilian defence staff. We are going to discuss all of that when we analyse the individual counts of the indictment, and now I would just like to add a few words to what my colleague Mr. Pantelic said with regard to joint criminal enterprise. I must say that although we were far away when writing our closing arguments, I wrote mine in Belgrade and he wrote his in The Hague, nevertheless, I must say that I fully subscribe to what Mr. Pantelic said here during his closing arguments. In the final brief, we already said what we believe is the case with regard to joint criminal enterprise. It seems that the Prosecution is aware of the fact that they did not think about this at the beginning of the trial, and this theory of joint criminal enterprise came to rise in other trials before this Tribunal. However, the fact that during this trial they came up with the idea to use this theory of joint criminal enterprise does not justify what they did. They did not articulate this theory either in their pre-trial brief or in their opening statement or in any of the amended indictments. As Mr. Pantelic said, they did not state this in any one of the four or rather five amended indictments. They waited for their case to come to an end, and it is only then that when we acted in respect of Rule 98 bis, asking for acquittal, then they chose to deal with this. The Defence claims, and we wrote about this in our brief, that the very words "working in concert together or with others" does not mean anything but co-perpetration, and that would also be my response to Judge Williams's question, the question put to Mr. Pantelic. Co-perpetration is something, but joint criminal enterprise is a completely different thing. The Prosecution amended their indictment twice during the trial itself. After the appeal judgement was passed in the Tadic case, as well as the Kvocka, Krnojelac, Krstic and Kordic judgements, and they did not dare present a clear-cut indictment as they waited for many witnesses to come and go. The Prosecution waited for Stevan Todorovic to testify. They thought that he was a key witness, but they did not articulate their theory before this statement. For this Prosecution, Stevan Todorovic is a key witness for joint criminal enterprise. That is why in its final brief the Defence invoked judicial practice, the rights of the accused from the Statute, and we said that such a thesis should not be accepted because this would infringe upon one of the fundamental rights to defence from Article 21 of the Statute. In paragraph 725 of the Kupreskic indictment, says -- it is said that the accused has to be informed of legal charges brought against an individual. The Prosecution did not do this, consciously or unconsciously, as Pantelic said, but perhaps this was done by omission too. However, that is something that should not reflect upon the accused. The accused has to be fully informed about the legal aspects of the charges brought against them. However, in addition to these procedural objections, but we consider them to be objections of substance as well, we are going to present our arguments in view of the Prosecution's thesis that Miroslav Tadic was a participant in joint criminal enterprise. The Defence claims that Miroslav Tadic was not aware of any plan or policy to persecute non-Serbs so as to ethnically cleanse or, rather, ethnically delineate between the Serb people and other peoples. Not at a single point in time did the accused come to realise that such a plan existed, if it existed at all, that it was prepared, implemented, and therefore he could not have taken part in the implementation of this plan. Since he was not aware of this plan, he could not show any kind of voluntariness in terms of supporting such a plan or actively participating in it. The Prosecution has claimed that these plans were secret ones. They are being related to structures of policy and government. Also the Prosecution has relied on testimony of politicians and in the intelligence community. Not a shred of evidence was presented with regard to Miroslav Tadic's awareness of this plan. There is no immediate evidence that he said that to someone or that somebody had told him that he had heard about it or indirect evidence that somebody had heard about that for him. Tadic was not in any political or party structures and he could not therefore be related to this plan. He was not a member of the security community or the intelligence community, and that is what the Prosecution refers to when referring to this plan. Mr. Pantelic mentioned a few minutes ago his own analysis of the document related to the strategic interests of the Serb people. It is questionable whether this is a discriminatory document, but obviously the Prosecution finds it a very important document and relies on it in order to talk about this kind of forced ethnic delineation. At the beginning, Your Honours, when Mr. Donia testified we insisted that this document fully be translated, precisely because of the date of this document, when it was published in the Official Gazette. Mr. Pantelic referred to it, so I'm not going to go back to that particular matter. The Prosecutor also refers to the statements of Marko Tubakovic and his concept of ethnic cleansing and forcible departures. However, this same Marko Tubakovic had the Prosecutor wanted to read his cross-examination, said something that completely changes what the Prosecution alleges. When the Defence attorneys presented to him the procedures applied during exchanges and when he had previously stated that he was never present, not during a single exchange, he agreed with the fact that there was no coercion, as far as exchanges were concerned. When awareness of a plan cannot be proven through direct or -- direct evidence, then the Prosecutor cannot rely upon anything else but providing a generalised analysis of evidence and also certain allegations. Now, what is the Prosecution offering? The Prosecution offers Tadic's vital role in the forcible takeover of government through activities in the 4th Detachment, that he took part in the supervision of arms collections, and that allegedly he was then in the company of paramilitaries, volunteers, whoever. We know who they're referring to. The handover of weapons was not carried out at all in the way in which the Prosecution wishes to present this. All evidence has shown that this was done in a way which the Prosecution does not find suitable. There is another thing I wish to point out: Not then or later was Tadic ever in the company of paramilitaries. However, if, according to the Prosecution, this is an element upon which it bases his participation in joint criminal enterprise, then the Prosecution is on thin ice in this case. In addition to the arbitrary allegations made by certain witnesses whose testimonies we have analysed in our brief, about Tadic's alleged presence in the company of the paramilitaries on those days, the Prosecutor forgets what was said about the relationship between Miroslav Tadic and those Specials, paramilitaries, during this trial. I will, however, have to remind the Prosecutor of that. Would anyone spend time with the very same people who forced him to humiliate himself in his own cafe by erasing Tito's name from the wall of an adjacent building? Would anyone want to socialise with dubious characters who break into his flat at night and force him to sign statements in Cyrillic? Several days ago, or yesterday, the Prosecutor quoted Tadic himself as saying to these characters: Do you know who I am? But the Prosecutor refused to include in the quote the following sentence, explaining why Tadic said that, and we don't know the answer that the man -- but we don't know the answer that the man gave. The man said: "We don't know who you are, but the one who has sent us knows." Now, did these people simply back off or give up after Tadic said that? No. He was forced to write the statement. He was searched for weapons. And later, they were wondering why Tadic was still alive at all. When Miroslav Tadic testified in February this year, he knew that that man's name was Zvjezdan. Now he has also found out that the first name is Zvjezdan and the last name is Jovanovic. He saw his photograph. We have heard testimonies about the maltreatment he suffered at this hand of Lugar, Laki, and Grof. I will remind the Prosecutor of the testimony concerning Captain Jez, who refused to allow the Serbs having the last name of Tadic to be exchanged. This is the very same Jez who was mentioned as having very close ties to Stevan Todorovic. What was Tadic's relationship with Stevan Todorovic, the man who arrested him? The man Tadic reported to the relevant offices from the military commission after the bloodbath, this man who was the Prosecutor's key witness, Todorovic, before the exchange in 1993. Let us just think about Salkic, Grujicic, and Maslic, and the documents testifying to that. How can it be that, as the Prosecutor claims, that Tadic and Todorovic socialised within this framework of a common joint enterprise when Tadic had to take advantage of his absence to win Cancarevic's approval to have Witness A exchanged? Who was it after all this evidence that wanted to sell the witness, according to the one-to-100 principle, and who was the man who finally had the man finally exchanged according to the one-for-one principle? All the documents that we have testified to the truthfulness of this. The Prosecutor goes on to claim that Tadic participated in the crucial early decisions of the Crisis Staff. I will have to repeat this sentence, because I don't think the transcript reflects accurately what I said. How much exactly did Tadic and Todorovic cooperate and socialise within the framework of this joint criminal enterprise according to the allegations by the Prosecution, when my client, Miroslav Tadic, had to take advantage of his absence in order to obtain Cancarevic's approval, who was the chief of the police station, to have Witness A exchanged? And who, after all this evidence, was the man who wanted to trade this witness or sell him, according to the one-man-for-100-men principle, as Todorovic speaks about, and who was the man who eventually exchanged him, according to the one-man-for-one-man principle? I mean, all the witnesses that we had that testified to this, this was in Lipovac in 1992, we have all the lists related to that exchange, those who left and those who stayed. The Prosecutor goes on to claim that Tadic took part in the crucial early decisions of the Crisis Staff. The problem for the Prosecution here is procedural. Miroslav Tadic was not charged with participation in any discriminatory decisions. If that had been the Prosecution's allegation, they would have had to indict him for it. It would have had to be one of the charges. He was a member of the Crisis Staff, but he is not specifically indicted for persecution, for this particular act of persecution. Blagoje Simic, on the other hand, is indicted, is charged with that, in paragraph 13b. Stevan Todorovic too was charged with an act of persecution, and he was found guilty, and the judgement clearly stated that Stevan Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff, and Milan Simic too was charged with this, in a different form, though, not that he was making discriminatory decisions but rather he was carrying out discriminatory decisions, and he also was alleged to have been a member of the Crisis Staff. Miroslav Tadic was a member of the Crisis Staff, but this incrimination, which must be strictly specified, we know the appeals judgement in the Kupreskic case and what it has to say about that. He has simply not been charged with that. And we can't have the Prosecution now, in their final argument, refer to something that our client has not been charged with. The Court can only decide on the charges which are actually in the indictment. There is another part of that sentence, the sentence that the Prosecution has referred to, indicating that the Prosecution finally accepted something that I was expecting them, I must say, to refer to, both in their final brief and in their closing arguments. The Prosecution said Miroslav Tadic participated in the early and, as they say, decisive or key decisions made by the Crisis Staff. I assume the Prosecution finally adopted the position that Miroslav Tadic was merely a member of the Crisis Staff, as the Defence has already claimed, in the period between the 23rd of April and July, when the War Presidency was established. Where did the Prosecutor claim that Tadic voluntarily and consciously was a member of such a criminal enterprise? There was not a single reference by the Prosecutor to that. Why, I'm asking myself. The answer was clear: Because there was not a single proof that they had. Just a brief conclusion, a couple of words along the same lines. On the basis of everything that we set out in our final brief, as well as the Prosecution's closing arguments and final brief, the Defence believes that the Prosecution failed to specifically present our client Tadic with the legal and factual allegations in connection with Tadic's participation in the joint criminal enterprise. In this way, the right of the accused to an appropriate defence was violated, which affected the Defence's cross-examination of several witnesses and the presentation of our evidence. On the other hand, they did not offer a single proof that Miroslav Tadic was aware of the plan or any proof of the alleged common goal which is required to prove the theory of the joint criminal enterprise. I will now pass to my colleague Mr. Krgovic. I would just like to say several words about Mr. Pantelic's words relating to international armed conflict and elements required for discrimination, that's forced labour and deportation, as the elements required for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. The Defence shall now proceed to discuss the responsibility of Miroslav Tadic as seen by the Prosecutor and the attitude of the Defence as regards count 1 of the indictment, persecution and the forcible takeover by the Serb forces in Samac municipality. At the very outset, the Defence believes it's necessary to say that we believe that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Miroslav Tadic participated in the forcible takeover of power in Bosanski Samac municipality in April 1992. The Defence has offered ample evidence showing the whereabouts of Miroslav Tadic during the days preceding and following April 1992 and what his activities were. We address this issue in our final brief. However, we want to point out once again that the Prosecution has failed to offer a single proof indicating Miroslav Tadic's participation in the preparations for the forcible takeover or his participation in the planning or any other activity which followed from that. The only thing that seems clear from the Prosecutor's final brief as to their view of the role of Miroslav Tadic in the preparations for the forcible takeover, the Prosecution addresses this in paragraph 109 of their final brief when they talk about the meeting that was held in the village of Struke, and Miroslav Tadic's presence at that meeting. They refer to the testimony of Witness Blaz Paradzik, which, in our view and the view of the Defence, is illogical and unconvincing, especially where he claims that the meeting was held on the 29th of February, 1992. Witness Paradzik claims that the meeting was held in the early morning hours on the 29th of February, 1992, between 11.00 and 12.00 in the morning. On the 29th of February, the inaugural session or founding assembly of the Serbian municipality of Samac in Pelagicevo was held in the village of Obudovac, which is about 40 kilometres from the village of Struke. So why would Blagoje Simic attend an insignificant meeting in the village of Struke, where purely local problems were discussed, on the same day when a very important meeting was held, which the Prosecution has agreed with. And during the time that the Serbian assembly was in session for one whole day. Why would Blagoje Simic have come to that meeting at that time? The session of the Serbian assembly of Samac should then have begun at 7.00 in the morning and should have taken one or two hours, at most, for him to be able to make it to the other meeting. And along the road, so to speak, to meet Rajko Djuric and Miroslav Tadic from Samac and bring them with him to that meeting. With all due respect, this is simply impossible. During the Defence case, witness Mitar Nijemcevic was heard, which Mr. Pantelic spoke about today. We're talking about depositions 403 to 401. Unlike witness Paradzik, witness Nijemcevic dated this meeting to mid-March, when the meeting was held. He remembered every single detail, the names of the persons present, the subjects discussed by each of the participants and where each of the individual participants were actually seated. Allow me please to refer to the page numbers, the page numbers are 403 through 421. Witness Nijemcevic was very cogent, convincing, and logical, and he dated this event to back in mid-March 1992, the day when the Serb women and children left the village of Struke, which sounds convincing, very convincing, and it makes his whole testimony credible, because it makes the time frame given, the time frame related to the women and children leaving the village of Struke, credible. Unlike Nijemcevic, Blaz Paradzik failed to remember a whole lot of details. He did not know -- he did not remember where the meeting was held or who was present. Blaz Paradzik gave statements to the OTP's investigators before he appeared before this Trial Chamber. He was cross-examined by Mr. Tadic's Defence. During this cross-examination, he was asked why in his previous statement he had never referred to the presence of Miroslav Tadic there, and then Blaz Paradzik lied, that he had referred to Mr. Tadic's presence but obviously the unconscientious investigators of the OTP failed to record that statement. This is on page 8249 of the transcript. In their final brief, the Prosecution claims that Blaz Paradzik's statement was not challenged during cross-examination, which is simply not true. What I just talked about clearly shows that Blaz Paradzik was thoroughly cross-examined and that that particular portion of his testimony was indeed challenged. If the Prosecutor wished to place Miroslav Tadic in the context of planning of forcible takeover, why upon cross-examination did they not ask him a single question related to his presence at Nijemcevic's house? Why did they not check Paradzik's and Nijemcevic's testimonies, both of whom testified before Tadic, and asked these questions? Their reference to witness Blaz Paradzik as their only means of support for that particular statement is very flimsy basis for the allegation that Miroslav Tadic had any participation or awareness of the existence of a plan for a forcible takeover. The meeting in the village of Struke is simply not as important as Paradzik tried to show. This is absolutely clear, because all Prosecution witnesses who described pre-war meetings failed to mention this particular meeting. This clearly points to the fact that this was a total insignificant, local meeting in a remote village, at which Tadic and Simic happened to be at the same time. Furthermore -- Let me just make a correction for the sake of the transcript. I said which happened at different times, page 129, line 7. Furthermore, the Prosecution attaches great importance to the collection of illegal weapons which was carried out on the 18th of April, 1992 by members of the 4th Detachment. Many witnesses have addressed this issue, as has the Defence, in our final brief. But we would like to address the claims made in paragraph 125 by the Prosecution in their final brief. They have made an enormous effort to make credible the testimony of Witness Esad Dagovic, especially as regards footnote 193, referring to his testimony. I will address Esad Dagovic's testimony, although we have discussed this in our final brief; the Trial Chamber has heard this testimony several times. In our submission, Your Honours, the only thing that was truthful that the witness actually said before the Court was maybe his first name, the last name, and the date of his birth. His testimony begins with a description of his own financial assets which he also referred to in his statement to the Prosecution, his fabulous riches, which can only be expressed in millions. The Prosecutor realised how unconvincing this was and they made corrections during the witness's examination-in-chief and then a photograph of his house was shown as the witness was talking about his considerable assets, the land he owned, the gold he owned, and then going on to describe Radovan Karadzic's and Vojislav Seselj's visit to Bosanski Samac. We have not heard a single witness testify to this effect. And then eventually the story that the Serbs bombarded the centre of Samac themselves. It is simply all false and untruthful. The Prosecution tries to take part of his statement out of the context. The defendant Simo Zaric suggesting it to the witness, putting it to the witness that he had several different types of armoured vehicles mixed up, the BOV and the tank whereas the witness was clear in statement he could distinguish between a Praga, a BOV, and a tank and that the distinction for him was crystal clear. The witness was cross-examined by the Defence and to a large extent his testimony proved false and his credibility was ruined. However, the Prosecution exhibited photographs along with a statement made by witness Richard Phillips, according to Rule 92 bis and to cover for the lies uttered by this witness in this way. The Prosecutor says in his final brief that these photographs show how a lay witness can easily confuse types of combat armoured vehicles, armoured vehicles, rather. However, witness Esad Dagovic clearly distinguished between different kinds of armoured vehicles and he did distinguish between Pragas, ACV, and tanks respectively. He showed an amazing knowledge concerning artillery weapons, especially multiple rocket launchers. Witness Esad Dagovic did his military service, has this knowledge, and I can say that he was showing off his knowledge here. I can certainly say that he was not a layman. Witness Esad Dagovic is not a layman; he is, quite simply, a liar. The allegation made by the Prosecution in their final brief that the alleged testimony of Miroslav Tadic is opposite to the testimonies made by Radovan Antic, Jovo Savic, Stevan Nikolic, Simo Zaric -- I beg your pardon. The transcript did not reflect a sentence of mine when I said that Esad Dagovic is not a layman; he is, quite simply, a liar. That's what I said, and I would like the transcript to reflect that. Also, in paragraph 126, the Prosecution refers to the contradictory nature of Miroslav Tadic's statements, as well as statements made by members of the command of the 4th Detachment and Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. However, invoking contradiction is just wishful thinking on the part of the Prosecution. The Defence does not see any contradictory factors between the testimony of Miroslav Tadic and the statements made by those witnesses. Your Honours, I believe that it is time for the adjournment now.
